An oil tanker has caught fire after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media has reported.
Iran 's Revolutionary Guards Navy said the incident on Saturday morning occurred in the eastern section of the waterway.
The incident comes as two oil tankers on Friday collided with sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, triggering several large explosions. Tankers in recent weeks have attempted to navigate what were described as unauthorised routes in the waterway.
Iran has imposed restrictions on vessels seeking to pass through the Strait of Hormuz and has attacked ships it says violated those restrictions, as it seeks to assert control over the strategic waterway and exert pressure on the US.

articles.title_orig: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
articles.title_zh: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
articles.content_orig:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, and a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".
The Ukrainian leader's comments came after US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees that as unrealistic.
The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.
It is possible the American envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky said recently that the US mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.
Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.
So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public in order to re-open a discussion that had been considered all-but closed.
He maintains that the idea is now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security.
It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.
The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.
Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.
He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".
In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".
He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.
The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.
Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service , which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.
Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

articles.title_orig: U.S. facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Russia amid push for peace in Ukraine, Kushner says
articles.title_zh: U.S. facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Russia amid push for peace in Ukraine, Kushner says
articles.content_orig:
Kaja Kallas says Moscow is trying to divert attention from its aggression by raising issue of European security
The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.
“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US was held this week in Abu Dhabi.
Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.
European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.
Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.
The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.
Speaking after a summit of EU leaders in Dublin on Friday, the European Council president, António Costa, said leaders had agreed on a negotiating team: the EU institutions and E5 countries, namely Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland.
“Europe must speak with one clear and united voice in all discussions that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent,” he said. “This is ultimately a team effort.”
The format had already emerged in recent months, but the need to formalise the grouping gained momentum after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, this week urged his European allies to decide who will represent Europe in negotiations.
Kushner also mocked the absence of a single person to speak for the entire continent. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations,” he said earlier this week.
after newsletter promotion
But there was an increasingly settled view that Europe would not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent. Paris and Berlin had argued for a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: Costa and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Earlier in the day, Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.
Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”
Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing , a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Netanyahu says it's time to remove Iran threat "once and for all"
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Netanyahu says it's time to remove Iran threat "once and for all"
articles.content_orig:
Mossad Director Roman Gofman is in Washington for talks, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The talks between the U.S. and Israel's foreign intelligence agency come at a time of great tension with Iran and amid reports that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking a renewal of war with Tehran.
The source did not confirm the subject of the talks.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed nine officials on Saturday, following an investigation into allegations of oil smuggling in the Jurf al-Sakher area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group.
"In light of the investigation's findings," Zaidi "ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary," his military spokesman Sabah al-Numan said, without identifying the suspects.
The premier "also ordered the dismissal" of nine officials including from the security and oil sectors.
The northern reaches of Iraq has several Shia Muslim militia groups that support Iran, a majority Shia country. The semi-autonomous groups have routinely launched missiles or drones at Middle Eastern countries in opposition to Iran's interests.
The U.S. and Saudi Arabia, a Sunni majority country and regular target of the Iraqi breakaway groups, launched joint strikes on northern Iraqi groups in July.
Invoking Iran's pursuit to rebuild its nuclear program, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Saturday it's time to eliminate the threat from Iran "once and for all" in a speech about forming a new government following a meeting earlier this week with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot.
"The Iranian regime, which seeks to destroy Israel, is once again working to revive its nuclear program," Netanyahu said, translated from Hebrew. "And let this be clear: This murderous regime, which did not hesitate to murder many thousands of its own people, will not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us."
"It will do so the moment it manages to resume uranium enrichment and the accelerated development of nuclear weapons," he continued.
Netanyahu said he met with Eisenkot on Thursday, and the meeting "only strengthened my understanding of how essential it is to establish a national unity government at this time."
In last month's election , Netanyahu's Likud party and its allies received 53 seats in the Knesset, short of the 61 needed to form a government and keep him as prime minister. Eisenkot's Yashar party and its allies won 48 seats, while the Arab coalition took 19 seats.
Netanyahu wondered aloud why Eisenkot would potentially side with the Arab coalition to form what he called a "fragile and dangerous government." Netanyahu is clinging to hopes Eisenkot will agree to a deal to establish a majority and cut out the Arab parties, who he has accused of stealing the election . On Saturday, he referred to them as "supporters of terrorism."
"We must remove this existential threat from over our heads once and for all," Netanyahu said, referring to Iran. "A narrow government, or a government that relies on supporters of terrorism, will not be able to achieve this monumental goal. But a national unity government can achieve it in time, thereby ensuring Israel's security for many years to come."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthi militant group said it intercepted and destroyed two drones on Saturday.
The drones were intercepted near Riyadh and over the southern region. The coalition was not more specific about where in the south it had been intercepted. Riyadh, the country's capital, is located in central Saudi Arabia, though hundreds of miles from the Houthis' base of operations in Yemen.
It was a busy week of drone and missile interceptions by the Saudis. The two drones intercepted on Saturday afternoon were the first since one was fired at the eastern, oil-rich region of the country on Thursday. Multiple drones in the east and near Riyadh were interrupted Thursday, while two ballistic missiles were shot down on Wednesday in the western part of Saudi Arabia and three others were shot down near Riyadh, according to the coalition.
Two drones were also intercepted on Wednesday, the coalition said, though one destroyed near Mecca was disavowed by the Houthis, who have said they will not target the holy city.
Multiple drones, ballistic missiles and cruise missiles were also intercepted over different parts of Saudi Arabia on Monday, the same day the coalition said it took out a weapons manufacturing facility in Yemen.
Iran and the United States should "immediately" allow fertilizer shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to ease the crisis in some of the most vulnerable countries, a senior U.N. official said Saturday.
Jorge Moreira da Silva, head of the U.N. Office for Project Services, told the COP31 climate talks in the Turkish resort city of Antalya that the lack of fertilizers could push millions into poverty.
While Iran and the United States are still trying to negotiate an end to the conflict, Moreira da Silva said he had the same message for both countries.
"They should continue their negotiations about the comprehensive deal — but that deal should not avoid an immediate, exceptional, limited, and time-bound solution for the fertilizers," he said.
"Basically what we need is five vessels a day with fertilizers," he added.
Before the conflict, a third of the world's fertilizers passed through the Strait of Hormuz, and since the blockades, their prices had risen by 30%, Moreira da Silva said.
Sudan's finance minister recently told him the price of food there had doubled in six months, he added. In Nepal, they told him that farmers could no longer afford to buy fertilizers.
"So it's very important that we are aware that countries such as Mozambique, Kenya, Sudan, Somalia, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka are facing very significant impact," Moreira da Silva said.
The effects of this shortage could be catastrophic, he warned.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps claims to have shot down an American MQ-1 "Predator" drone for the second straight day on Saturday.
This was the 17th MQ-1 drone shot down by Iran, according to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, though that number was not possible to verify. The U.S. certainly has lost a number of the drones, however, either to them being shot down or crashing.
The drone was shot down over Iran's Qeshm Island, which is located along the northern coast of the Strait of Hormuz. Like Friday, the strike was credited to Iran's alleged new air defense system.
The U.S. has lost dozens of unmanned aircraft during the war with Iran, according to a congressional report dated Oct. 5. Forty-five MQ-9 Reaper drones have been lost, just through mid-August, while at least three Predator drones were previously destroyed, according to the report.
There were at least 81 manned or unmanned aircraft lost during the war in Iran through early October, according to the report. As of Aug. 1, the losses amounted to a cost of between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion.
Iran's military said on Saturday that fires had broken out on a total of three oil tankers that struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has insisted vessels obtain its authorization to cross the strait since war erupted with the United States in February, and has attacked ships that do not comply.
"A short while ago, two oil tankers that had switched off their radar and positioning systems and were secretly attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized route exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine," the Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement on the incident in the south of the waterway, carried by the Iranian state broadcaster early on Saturday.

articles.title_orig: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever
articles.title_zh: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever
articles.content_orig:
After a booster explosion on Friday, SpaceX successfully caught the upper stage, or spacecraft, portion of its massive Starship rocket from orbit on Saturday — a triumphant milestone for the company.
SpaceX made the historic catch using its "chopsticks," mechanical arms attached to a launch tower, at its facility in Starbase, Texas.
Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship test yet, marked the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the rocket's booster and upper stage.
Musk posted a video on X inspecting the upper stage craft after completing the capture.
During the first phase of the test flight on Friday, SpaceX failed to catch and recover the booster, instead diverting it to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded before hitting the water.
The rocket's upper stage then continued into orbit and flew around the Earth 14 times before successfully landing on SpaceX's launch tower, nicknamed Mechazilla.
The Hawaii Department of Transportation issued a temporary pause on some West Coast flights Friday, due to debris risk from the flight. Separately, the FAA issued a rare, nationwide ground stop due to telecommunications system failures. (Both of those orders have since been lifted.)
Making Starship a reliable and fully reusable rocket is critical to SpaceX's ambitions. In the near term, the company needs Starship to send more satellites into orbit to expand its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center.
SpaceX is also expected to use Starship to bring astronauts and cargo from lunar orbit to the Moon's surface and back for NASA . Musk also has a grand vision to use Starship to "colonize Mars" and "make humanity multi-planetary."
During Test Flight 15 on Friday, SpaceX released another 26 of its newest Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, growing its commercial satellite internet network.
The company's constellation already included over 11,000 satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket can carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites, the company has said.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX successfully catches part of Starship rocket on its return to Earth
articles.title_zh: SpaceX successfully catches part of Starship rocket on its return to Earth
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time.
"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.
The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.
But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.
The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:27 local time (21:27 GMT) on Saturday and was successfuly caught.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Carried a Secret for More Than a Year. It Led to His Downfall.
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Carried a Secret for More Than a Year. It Led to His Downfall.
articles.content_orig:
President Trump suggested on Thursday that Tim Cook, former CEO of Apple, should become the leader of chip maker Nvidia following its chief executive Jensen Huang ’s resignation over his alleged affairs with two women.
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend! ” Trump posted on TruthSocial.
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday morning, in the wake of reports that he had allegedly been involved in two affairs, including one with a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy.
It is unclear if Trump has reached out to Cook regarding this suggestion. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Huang and the White House have maintained a close relationship since the start of Trump’s second term. During his official visit to China in May, Trump invited Huang to attend the summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The New York Times reported that the President insisted on inviting Huang to join the delegation despite concerns over Huang’s relationship with a woman who is believed to be a Chinese spy.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, Trump repeatedly downplayed Huang’s alleged affair, insisting that he believed the tech billionaire’s assertion that he knew nothing about the alleged espionage operation.
“I really believe him,” Trump told reporters during the White House press conference. “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

articles.title_orig: Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping expected to meet in first-ever trilateral of its kind, officials say
articles.title_zh: Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping expected to meet in first-ever trilateral of its kind, officials say
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping will hold the first three-way meeting among the three leaders at a summit in China next week, the White House said Friday.
The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The Kremlin also confirmed the meeting on Saturday.
Mr. Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks and is also set to bring up the war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine , officials said.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.
One of the major conflicts dominating Mr. Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the U.S. officials said.
"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that U.S. envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.
Mr. Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday — their fourth meeting since the president's return to power last year.
The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.
"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.
Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk will accompany Mr. Trump on his trip to China but will not be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.
Mr. Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen.
Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which then-U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain's Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations after World War II.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can't be enforced on others.
"It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant," Peskov said. "However, let's not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect."
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Bay Area Denny's now reinstalling plaque commemorating Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: Bay Area Denny's now reinstalling plaque commemorating Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
Amidst the scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the original Denny’s location where he once worked removed the plaque that celebrated his success.
Amidst the scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the original Denny's location where he once worked removed the plaque that celebrated his success. On Friday, the restaurant announced it was reinstalling it.
The plaque was presented on Sept. 26, 2023 , by the CEO of Denny's, Kelli Valade, highlighting the very booth Huang conceived his idea for Nvidia. The plaque was removed as of Thursday, but on Friday, the company announced it was reinstalling it.
Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are
Denny’s released the following statement on the matter:
“We’re reinstalling the plaque recognizing the conversations at Denny’s that helped launch NVIDIA.
Jensen Huang started at Denny’s as a dishwasher. Years later, he and his co-founders gathered in one of our booths to discuss the idea that became NVIDIA. The plaque commemorates that shared history. America’s Diner has long been a place where people and ideas come together, and that history deserves to be preserved.”
On Thursday, Huang resigned from his duties at Nvidia. On the same day, Nvidia shares fell by more than 4%, according to the Associated Press.
The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman suspected to be a Chinese spy by U.S. Intelligence. On Sunday, Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised by this affair.
Still, lawmakers in Washington D.C. are calling for further investigations on the matter. President Donald Trump confirmed the FBI is looking into the affair.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi. File
                                          | Photo Credit: Reuters
Prime Minister Narendra Modi will meet U.S. President Donald Trump, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the first Quad Summit since 2024 this week in Manila, on the sidelines of ASEAN summits, sources in New Delhi confirmed to The Hindu . The meeting is expected to take place on November 17 evening, the sources said, adding that it would probably take place after Mr. Trump lands in Manila.
While the confirmation of the Quad Summit in Manila is significant for the Indo-Pacific grouping, and plans to chart out their next course, much of the attention will be taken by Mr. Trump’s pronouncements at his next stop in Shenzhen, China, where he will hold the first-ever three-way summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on November 19, to discuss global issues including nuclear arms control.
In Washington, U.S. officials briefing media on Mr. Trump’s travels also confirmed that the US President will travel to Manila and, among other meetings, will take part in a “multilateral meeting” with Quad country leaders, news agency Reuters reported.
The agency quoted an official briefing by unnamed officials who said that supply chains for critical minerals and securing commercial shipping lanes for energy supplies would be a key part of the agenda. “The issue of attacks on commercial ships is very likely to ​be taken up,” the unnamed official quoted by Reuters said. The safety of ships and seafarers has been a particularly important issue for India, as at least 30 Indian seafarers aboard ships in the Hormuz Strait, the Sea of Oman, and the Black Sea have been killed in attacks during the conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, respectively.  Earlier, reports had indicated that a Quad Business Forum mechanism would also be announced during the Summit.
The Manila meeting will be the first Quad Summit to be held in a non-Quad country and indicates the challenges that India has faced as the Chair of the Summit of the four-country grouping that revived its cooperation in the Indo-Pacific in 2017, upgrading it during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021 to leader-level meetings. Since then, the government has been unable to host the Quad Summit in India even once, mainly due to the U.S. President’s unavailability. New Delhi is unwilling to hand over the Chairship of the summit without hosting it here either, which may yet happen in Delhi next year, the sources told The Hindu .
Officials didn’t clarify on who will be the official host of the meeting in Manila, which has been discussed for weeks, including during U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visits to India this year in May and October. The US midterm election results, in which the ruling Republican Party lost its majorities in the U.S. Congress, had delayed the confirmation of Mr. Trump’s travels to the Philippines for the East Asia Summit and to China for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit.
On Friday (November 13, 2026), when asked at a briefing, government spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told journalists only that the MEA would “keep [them] updated with developments in Manila pertaining to the Quad”. On Saturday (November 14, 2026) evening, officials who confirmed the Summit would take place late on Tuesday evening (November 17, 2026) said they were still awaiting a formal intimation of the timing.

articles.title_orig: Tech Leaders Rally Behind Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: Tech Leaders Rally Behind Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang."
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker.
Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing , with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June.
The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress , who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence.
"But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday amid multiple affair allegations, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang , who also worked with Nvidia customer Megaspeed . The Singapore-based company is being investigated by the Justice Department for possibly redirecting some of its supply of Nvidia's restricted artificial intelligence chips to China.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X Friday that he signed a petition asking to reinstate Huang. A petition circulating online called "Stand with Jensen" claims to have more than 100,000 signatures, including more than 5,000 current Nvidia employees.
Musk said on X Saturday that without Huang, some "critical deals will be lost."
Another letter sent Friday called on U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee.
Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 about whether the Commerce Department is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips," according to the letter. Huang has also been asked to testify .
The Commerce Department originally launched an investigation into Megaspeed that was moved to the Justice Department in 2025 after Nvidia's lawyer contacted a senior Commerce official, according to The New York Times.
President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit China on Thursday, but doesn't plan to raise Nvidia and the suspected spy affair during his meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping , according to U.S. officials. Musk is expected to join Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

articles.title_orig: Blumenthal says Lutnick ‘must go’ following Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: Blumenthal says Lutnick ‘must go’ following Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday accused the Commerce Department of a delay in labeling Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat, publicly airing an ongoing administration blame game following the ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
His comments come as some of President Donald Trump’s advisers, reeling from the fallout of Huang’s resignation, have begun discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be dismissed, according to people familiar with the conversations. Trump himself has also fielded calls from administration officials and outside advisors raising alarm bells about Lutnick, two additional people said.
So far, the White House has stood by him, issuing a statement Thursday – before Bessent’s comments – saying Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” Trump and Lutnick are longtime friends, and sources said it was unclear what the president might do.
Speaking on CNBC, Bessent said a wide swath of Trump’s administration — including the Treasury and State departments, the Pentagon and the US Trade Representative — favored placing Megaspeed on an export blacklist.
He said it was the Commerce Department, led by Lutnick, that had failed the follow through.
“Commerce…has the pen. You would have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.
He suggested the inaction had violated directives given by Trump.
“I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above” a certain technological level, he said.
“And so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, gives the Chinese an advantage,” he went on.
CNN has reached out to the Commerce Department for comment.
Trump officials have long harbored concerns that Megaspeed has circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China — a prospect that Treasury staffers argued should land it on Commerce’s so-called entity list of China-connected companies that could pose national security risks.
But the issue gathered newfound attention and importance in recent days when it was reported publicly that Huang had an affair with a Megaspeed employee suspected of having intelligence connections to China.
Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, were briefed months ago about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive.
Despite those warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list, people familiar with the matter said.
In a tense Situation Room meeting last week, Bessent challenged Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to blacklist Megaspeed, CNN previously reported. Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action, they said.
In the interview Friday, Bessent did not deny the confrontation .
“We don’t repeat conversations in the Situation Room,” he said.

Donald Trump will meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China next week for an unprecedented three-way meeting between the leaders of the US , Russia , and China, with nuclear weapons and the war in Iran expected to be on the agenda.
The meeting will take place on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, the White House confirmed on Friday. It will bring together the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers for the first time, although all three have held bilateral talks with one another.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The meeting comes nine months after the expiry of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), the last major nuclear arms control agreement between Washington and Moscow.
The treaty, which expired in February, had placed limits on the two countries’ strategic nuclear arsenals, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear powers without those restrictions for the first time in more than half a century.
Mr Trump has rejected Russia's offer to extend it for another year, saying he wanted a new agreement that would also include China.
Beijing has resisted joining such negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal is much smaller than those of Washington and Moscow. China has more than 600 nuclear warheads, compared with more than 5,000 each for Russia and the US.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told reporters, according to Reuters. “This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think ​it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have ​adult conversations about adult things.”
Mr Trump also intends to discuss the war in Iran with Mr Xi and Mr Putin, but Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not expected to feature, the official said. “We’ve had many meetings ⁠recently with ​the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, ​so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly insisted that his country must be involved in any discussions about its future.
Russia had previously proposed the three-way meeting, with Mr Putin reportedly keen to use it to discuss Ukraine. The Russian president had floated the idea during a telephone conversation with Trump last month, according to the Wall Street Journal .
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha had warned against giving Putin such a platform. “Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandisement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” he said last month, adding that it would only “encourage Putin to continue this war”.
The planned summit has also drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union discussed the postwar settlement in Europe. The prospect of Mr Trump, Mr Putin, and Mr Xi meeting without Ukraine has revived concerns about major powers making decisions that affect other countries without consulting them.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the comparison, saying that any agreements reached in Shenzhen could not be imposed on other countries. He nevertheless described a meeting between the three leaders as “extremely significant”. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect,” he said.
Mr Trump is due to visit Manila on Tuesday for talks with leaders of the Association of South-east Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen. He is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks and a working lunch with Xi on Thursday, ahead of the trilateral meeting.
The White House said billionaire Elon Musk would accompany Mr Trump on the China visit, but a senior US official said he would not attend the talks with Mr Xi and Mr Putin.

articles.title_zh: US aviation shutdown blamed on L3 Harris installed router
articles.content_orig:
Read live updates on Saturday flight cancellations and delays here .
• Ground stop: Domestic US flights are being allowed to depart again after federal officials issued an hours-long ground stop due to safety concerns from a telecommunications outage . Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy blamed old air traffic control technology and overloaded routers.
• Update problem: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin pointed to FAA updates to those aging systems as the reason behind the halt. He added the ground stop did not stem from a threat to the US and was not linked to this week’s disruptive Microsoft outage.
• Call to Congress: Duffy warned of more disruption unless the system is updated, urging Congress to provide funds for improvements. It’s “going to be slow” to return to normal, he said , adding that it shouldn’t impact Thanksgiving travel in a couple weeks.
• Travel nightmare: Thousands of travelers face an uncertain night sleeping on airport floors or stuck in agonizingly long queues early Saturday. More than 15,000 US flights were either delayed or canceled on Friday, and about 3,000 are expected to be delayed or canceled on Saturday.
Major European airports have been impacted by the hours-long ground stop across the US, with some departures from airports, including Paris’s Charles de Gaulle (CDG) Airport and Germany’s Frankfurt Airport, showing as cancelled or delayed on Saturday.
The departure board of Paris’s CDG airport showed a Delta Airlines flight bound for Salt Late City, Utah, at 10.10 a.m. local time is cancelled, in addition to an American Airlines flight from the same airport to Dallas-Fort Worth in North Texas at 11.05 a.m. local time.
At Germany’s Frankfurt Airport, a flight scheduled to Atlanta at 10.30 a.m. local time has been cancelled, as has a flight bound for Detroit at 10.55 a.m. A separate flight from Frankfurt to Chicago was showing as delayed by nearly an hour, with a new scheduled departure time of 11.40 a.m.
Some other flights from Frankfurt Airport to destinations in the US appear to be running, including an 11.00 a. m. flight to New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport.
At Amsterdam Airport Schiphol, a flight due to depart for Chicago at 11.40 a.m. was showing as cancelled, with passengers instructed to call United Airlines for more information.
The UK’s Department for Transport has advised people travelling to the US to check with their airline before leaving for the airport.
Frustrated travelers will continue to face delayed or canceled flights and hours-long waits at US airports, as federal officials warned it will take time for airports and airlines to get back to full capacity following a massive grounding.
As yesterday’s FAA ground stop reminded the nation, flights get canceled and delayed at any time and for numerous reasons — from bad weather and mechanical issues to operational glitches.
Keep in mind that in the US, when an airline cancels your flight, you are entitled to a refund if you choose not to travel.
“If a flight does get canceled, travelers are owed a full refund for the ticket, full stop. If they are presented with a credit, they have the right to refuse and ask for monetary refund,” said Katy Nastro, a spokesperson for travel site Going.com , who was underlining Department of Transportation rules .
If a big storm or another complication seems poised to disrupt your flights, “look to make alternative travel plans immediately,” said Eric Napoli, chief legal officer at AirHelp , an air passenger rights company. Competition for seats becomes fierce during the holiday season when flights are more full.
“Travelers should consider looking at flights that are very early in the morning — as these are typically less delayed, too,” Napoli said.
Here’s more on what experts say you should do if your flight is delayed or canceled.
Thousands of travelers faced an uncertain night sleeping on airport floors or stuck in agonizingly long queues early Saturday, as many flights remained canceled across the country following a systems failure that grounded all US planes.
Flights resumed at 8:15 p.m. ET. But travel chaos is expected to continue into the weekend as airlines try to clear the huge volumes of displaced planes, passengers, luggage and crew.
• What happened: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop for all flights in the US Friday afternoon. A ground stop requires aircraft to remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when it was issued. The order was lifted more than four hours later.
• Travel nightmare: More than 15,000 US flights were either delayed or canceled on Friday and about 3,000 are expected to be delayed or canceled on Saturday, according to flight data tracker FlightAware. With so many aircraft unable to fly, airports ran out of gates and tarmac space to park planes. Some flights have resumed but huge crowds remain stranded at airports around the US as officials warned it will take time to clear the backlog.
• Why planes were grounded: The rare decision to halt all US flights was made after “incredibly old” air traffic control routers became overloaded with data and started to give inconsistent readings, US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the FAA added new technology into an existing framework, which overwhelmed the older system.
• System upgrade: Administration officials said more such incidents will happen until the system is upgraded. President Donald Trump pushed for Congress to pass legislation modernizing air traffic control towers, terminals and other critical infrastructure, according to a source. And Mullin called for a “complete overhaul” of the FAA’s technology systems, which he said could cost about $50 billion.
CNN’s Laura Sharman, Lucas Lilieholm, Kit Maher, Aleena Fayaz, Molly English, and Emma Tucker contributed reporting.
Images of stranded and frustrated passengers, planes crowding the tarmac, and airport departure boards lit up with red cancellation notices give a snapshot of the travel nightmare that unfolded across the United States on Friday and into Saturday.
Federal officials grounded all US flights for more than four hours due to safety concerns from a systems failure, saying an upgrade to old air traffic control technology that overloaded routers was to blame. Some flights have resumed, but further disruption is expected into the weekend.
Fixing the issues that led to Friday’s flight grounding is more complex than simply upgrading physical infrastructure, aviation safety expert David Soucie said after officials attributed the shutdown to outdated and overloaded systems.
Soucie told CNN that the real challenge lies in how these systems are interconnected and communicate with one another.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cited old air traffic control technology and overloaded routers as causes of the nationwide grounding, noting that it was not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system and affected only legacy equipment.
The FAA has already replaced thousands of copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of an overhaul that began last year, after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding, according to the Associated Press.
However, Soucie said that even when old copper wires are replaced, new vulnerabilities can arise. There was a reason copper was used for so long, he said.
“They can’t be changed, they can’t be modified, they can’t be hacked… so to change that and still maintain a constant system that’s not vulnerable to attack is not a simple task,” Soucie said.
Even the “basic structure of how things work together – they’re interdependent on each other – that takes an enormous amount of coordination.”

articles.title_orig: US Flight Chaos Spills Into Weekend After Nationwide Stoppage
articles.title_zh: US Flight Chaos Spills Into Weekend After Nationwide Stoppage
articles.content_orig:
Flight cancellations and delays disrupted operations at multiple U.S. airports Thursday.
As of 9:58 a.m. EST, there were at least 820 delays into or out of the United States, according to flight tracker FlightAware , and more than 10,261 worldwide.
FlightAware.com, which tracks live flight delay and cancellation statistics each day in real-time , reports another 65 U.S. flights had been canceled, and 456 worldwide.
Here's why so many flights were disrupted across the U.S.
Low clouds, rain and wind may delay or cancel flights in Boston (BOS), Chicago (MDW, ORD), New York (EWR, JFK, LGA), Philadelphia (PHL) and Washington, D.C. (BWI, DCA, IAD), according to the Federal Aviation Administration .
The FAA also noted that low clouds may disrupt flights in Houston (HOU, IAH) and San Francisco (SFO).
Afternoon showers and thunderstorms could also disrupt flights in Fort Lauderdale (FLL) and Miami (MIA).
If your flight is delayed or canceled, here are steps to reach your destination as quickly as possible.
Travel experts and airlines recommend the following steps if your flight is delayed or canceled.
Check your flight status regularly through your airline's website or app.
Download your airline's app and enable notifications for gate changes, delays and cancellations.
If your flight is canceled, rebook as soon as possible.
If you have a connecting flight, allow extra time if you're connecting through a busy airport.
Keep essential items in your carry-on for easy access during extended delays, and review your airline's refund and rebooking policies in case of extended delays or cancellations.
Josh Bandura, travel finance expert and co-founder of Frugal Flyer , shared some travel tips with Advance Local on what to do if caught in a flight delay or cancellation.
"The travelers who come out of a meltdown like this in decent shape are usually the ones who booked directly with the airline instead of through a third party, because the airline can only rebook a ticket it controls," Bandura said.
"Status helps too, mostly by moving you up the queue. My practical advice: work the app before you join the gate line, since rebooking options tend to appear there before an agent can offer them," he added.
"And if you're rebooked rather than refunded, don't treat the first option as final. There is often residual value left in the original ticket, and you have more rights than the agent has time to explain," Bandura continued.

articles.title_orig: What Travelers Caught in the Air-Travel Delays Need to Know
articles.title_zh: What Travelers Caught in the Air-Travel Delays Need to Know
articles.content_orig:
"The airlines are trying to get back to normal."
As air travel in the United States remains hectic due to the lingering effects from Friday's ground stop , a travel expert said preparation and patience are key for flyers who are trying to reach their destination.
Brett Snyder, the president of the travel planning service Cranky Concierge, said that flight schedules will likely not be back to normal until Monday at the earliest as airlines scramble to get their fleets and crews back to their planned destinations as orderly as possible.
A total of over 14,000 flights were canceled Friday and Saturday, according to FlightAware. Around 160 flights on Sunday have been canceled as of Saturday afternoon, FlightAware said.
The FAA said the ground stop was instituted due to a telecommunications issue in the air traffic control system.
FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the system is expected to be fully recovered by Sunday.
"The point of the cancellations and delays today is to right the ship as quick as possible and by Monday everything is as smooth as possible," Snyder told ABC News Saturday.
Snyder said that while there's not a lot passengers can do while the airlines and airports recover, there are key steps they can take to help ensure their flights go as smooth as possible.
The first thing that flyers should consider is if it's worth waiting for their flight if it has been delayed or if they should rebook, he said.
"If this was a trip that was going to be short and fun and not a big deal, I'd scrap it," Snyder said.
Snyder said that most airlines are offering refunds during this situation, even if their planned flight is delayed.
American Airlines announced Saturday it is adding fare caps across their domestic and short international flights as delays are expected to continue. American, Southwest, Delta and United are all offering travelers waivers.
For those who are still pushing ahead with their trip, Snyder said it's best to stay at the airport and remain on top of any updates. He recommended travelers download the airline's app and keeping an eye on all the alerts associated with their flight.
Snyder noted that flyers should pay close attention to any connecting flights and check if they are canceled. Airlines are typically good at rebooking customers during those situations, he added.
When in doubt, Snyder recommended that flyers call their airlines. If they are in the airport, talk to an agent, he said.
He stressed that ticket holders should remain courteous to the representatives.
"Remember the airline employees are going through this just as much you are as a traveler. Go easy on them, they're trying to help you," Snyder said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters Saturday that the federal government is working around the clock to help the airlines and airports navigate through the issues and get service back to normal as fast as possible.
"You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most," Duffy said in a post on X earlier Saturday.
"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," Duffy said.

articles.title_orig: Pentagon Pete Hegseth’s New Project Slammed as Brazen Self-Dealing in Lawsuit
articles.title_zh: Pentagon Pete Hegseth’s New Project Slammed as Brazen Self-Dealing in Lawsuit
articles.content_orig:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegsethâs pet project with Elon Musk and Newt Gingrich has been accused of turning the Pentagon into a playground for defense industry profiteers.
Government watchdog groups have filed a lawsuit claiming Hegsethâs âProject Meridianâ âan advisory committee he has tasked with identifying the militaryâs future weapons and technology needsâis violating federal law.
The lawsuit lands at an especially precarious moment for the Fox host-turned-defense secretary, who is simultaneously scrambling to convince President Donald Trump to keep him in the job while facing impeachment efforts in Congress.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is being floated as President Donald Trumpâs scapegoat for the Iran war debacle.
AARON SCHWARTZ/AFP via Getty Images
The complaint alleges that Hegsethâs project flouted several Federal Advisory Committee Act requirements, which are intended to prevent conflicts of interest while ensuring transparency, a balanced representation of viewpoints, and opportunities for public input.
The watchdogs argue that Project Meridian presents major conflicts of interest concerns because Hegseth has packed the committee with members who have financial stakes in the defense industry and stand to benefit from the recommendations they are tasked with making.
By clicking â SUBSCRIBE â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
The committee is led by Gingrich, Musk, and defense technology entrepreneur Palmer Luckey.
Hegseth chose two billionaires with stakes in the defense industry to lead the Pentagonâs study on the future of warfare.
The watchdogs cited Musk and Luckeyâs substantial government business, noting SpaceX has roughly $8 billion in defense contracts, while Luckeyâs Anduril Industries has around $25 billion.
âStacking Project Meridian with industry leaders will further skew national security policy toward corporate priorities, and away from the public interest,â one of the plaintiffs, the Project on Government Oversight, wrote in a statement .
Meanwhile, the lawsuit argues that the committee members without financial interests âdo not provide fair balance,â noting that Gingrich, 83, was the former Republican leader in the House and remains a close ally of Trump, who appointed Gingrichâs wife as U.S. ambassador to Switzerland and Liechtenstein last year.
âGiven everything I believe in, a large part of me thinks I should have gone over,â Gingrich said in a 1980s interview, reflecting on his decision not to serve in Vietnam. But he explained: âPart of the question I had to ask myself was what difference I would have made.â
Kevin Dietsch/Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
Gingrich is a curious choice for a committee tasked with studying the future of warfare, given that he avoided serving in the Vietnam War. He took deferments as a studentâgraduating from Emory University in 1965, and then Tulane in 1968 and 1971 with graduate degreesâwhile his status as a father pushed him further down the line for the draft. His wife at the time was his former high school math teacher, Jackie Battley, whom he later cheated on and divorced.
The lawsuit further alleges that Hegsethâs project violated the Federal Advisory Committee Act by failing to publish a Federal Register notice to allow public review and comment, and by failing to consult the General Services Administration on whether the project served the public interest.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: Iran state TV says modified missile could reach US base in Britain
articles.title_zh: Iran state TV says modified missile could reach US base in Britain
articles.content_orig:
Iranian state television has warned that modified versions of the country's Khorramshahr ballistic missile could reach American military bases in Europe, explicitly naming RAF Fairford in Britain as a potential target.
"The range of Iran's missiles is not limited to what they have seen," the report, broadcast Saturday, said, claiming that modifications to the Khorramshahr's warhead could increase its range severalfold.
The Khorramshahr-4, unveiled in 2023, has a claimed range of 2,000 kilometers while carrying a warhead weighing 1,500 kilograms. A lighter warhead could extend its range, although the extent of any increase remains unverified.
The broadcast included a review of missiles and drones Iran has used in its wars with Israel and the United States since June 2025, presenting the Khorramshahr as part of a broader arsenal capable of threatening American installations farther afield.
In a warning directed at Britain, the report suggested that British air defenses were not necessarily more capable than Israel's, which it claimed Iranian missiles had already penetrated during the war.
There has been no independent confirmation that Iran possesses a modified Khorramshahr capable of reaching RAF Fairford.
The broadcast invoked an order by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei that Iran's armed forces should face no geographical restrictions in responding to attacks by the United States or Israel.
Khamenei issued the directive on October 31, calling for immediate and effective retaliation without geographical limits and ordering military commanders to update their list of potential targets.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards subsequently said the country's longstanding self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometers on ballistic missile ranges had been lifted, although they did not specify whether longer-range missiles had been developed or deployed.
The broadcast follows a series of warnings from senior Iranian officials that American bases in Europe and on distant islands could become targets if Washington launches further attacks.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said earlier this week that Tehran would no longer confine its response to nearby US military installations and could strike bases in European countries.
The threats come as diplomatic efforts to end the war remain stalled, with Tehran demanding an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and relief from sanctions before negotiations can resume.
Washington has maintained its economic pressure campaign, while President Donald Trump has declared that he wants a total victory over Iran and suggested the United States no longer needs a negotiated agreement.
The latest state television report went further than previous warnings by naming a specific British installation and linking the threat to a purportedly extended-range version of the Khorramshahr missile.
“The Iranian people and the Israeli people, we love each other, we support each other,” Haddad said in Iran International’s Washington studio. “Every place I went for a demonstration, for a protest, I had Iranians at my back helping me.”
Haddad, a Christian from Nazareth and a volunteer Israeli army veteran, is one of Israel’s best-known advocates abroad. He ran second on Amcha Yisrael, a new right-wing list led by retired Brigadier General Ofer Winter, in Israel’s October 27 election. The list won 1.68 percent of the vote and no seats.
Haddad said he wanted to turn the ties between ordinary Israelis and Iranians into a common campaign.
“My plan is to take that relationship between the Israeli people and the Iranian people and strengthen it, and with the numbers, together we serve the same mission, which is one: destroying the IRGC and bringing security to Israel and the entire Middle East,” he said.
Israel has fought on what Haddad called seven fronts since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, including direct war with the Islamic Republic. In his view, Israel won militarily but stopped short of finishing the job, and the reason was the battle for public opinion.
“You know why we were stopped? Because of the public diplomacy and anti-Israel propaganda,” he said. “The way to fight the IRGC and to destroy the IRGC is through public diplomacy.”
He said Israel’s own government had fallen short. “We could have done more for Israeli public diplomacy. We could have done more for the Iranian people’s public diplomacy, and especially for the Iranian people against the IRGC,” he said.
He accused Qatar, which has hosted Hamas’s political office and funds Al Jazeera, of dominating that arena. “We completely gave that arena to Qatar, and they are shifting the narrative,” he said.
An Arab in the Israeli army
Haddad served in the Golani Brigade and was badly wounded by a Hezbollah anti-tank missile in the 2006 Lebanon war. “It was my Jewish brothers in arms who saved my life and who brought me back to Israel,” he said.
Arab citizens, about a fifth of Israel’s population, are exempt from compulsory service, and Haddad volunteered.
“I, as an Arab, was a commander over Jewish soldiers in the IDF,” he said, rejecting the charge that Israel is an apartheid state.
In 2024 he lit a torch at Israel’s official Independence Day ceremony. “This is something huge for an Israeli, yes, but for an Arab Israeli, it’s absolutely crazy,” he said.
Criticism of Arab-led parties
Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats in the October 27 election, and their backing helped opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot win the mandate to form a government. Haddad said the result showed Israel’s democracy works, but he accused the parties’ leaders of neglecting their own voters.
“When the election comes, all the leaders stop talking about Gaza, stop talking about Jenin and Ramallah, and finally they start talking again about Nazareth and Haifa,” he said. “They’re lying to us, time after time.”
He singled out Ahmad Tibi, the veteran head of Ta’al. “He tells you that Israel is an apartheid state. He tells you that he doesn’t want Israel as a Jewish state,”
He also said Tibi was protected by his parliamentary immunity. “He hit a cop, but because he’s a politician, he has immunity. No one can do anything to him,” Haddad said.
Haddad said he had once been kept out of a Knesset committee session chaired by Joint List lawmaker Aida Touma-Sliman on the claim that Israel is an apartheid state.
“I told her, ‘You guys are actually the apartheid, because you don’t want to listen to me, and I’m one of you, an Arab just like you,’” he said. “Pure apartheid toward me.”
He also cited Sami Abu Shehadeh, head of the Balad party, who withdrew from the election in October after the Central Elections Committee voted to bar him over remarks after the October 7 attack.
“They don’t want to set a precedent,” Haddad said of the Supreme Court, which recommended the withdrawal rather than ruling. “I’m all for freedom of speech, until you start to incite to terrorism.”
Haddad said the Guards’ proxies indoctrinate children from an early age, and that education can work in both directions. He praised the United Arab Emirates, which designated the Muslim Brotherhood a terrorist group in 2014 and later began teaching the Holocaust in schools.
Of children raised by Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon, he said: “When you arrive at age 12, you’re already serving in their terrorist organization, completely brainwashed. When you arrive at age 16, you’re ready to die.”
Haddad said he hoped Israelis and Iranians would build a common front.
"Together, the people of Israel and the people of Iran, we can actually do it," he said.

articles.title_orig: FAA ground stop lifted: NYC-airports facing delays, cancellations after communication issue
articles.title_zh: FAA ground stop lifted: NYC-airports facing delays, cancellations after communication issue
articles.content_orig:
The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop just after 8 p.m. on Friday
NEW YORK (WABC) -- Thousands of travelers across the New York area are grappling with the effects of a nationwide ground stop, with nearly 2,000 flights canceled across the country on Saturday.
The disruptions are being felt across the region at Newark Liberty International Airport, John F. Kennedy International Airport, and LaGuardia Airport, as passengers face delays, cancellations, and uncertain travel plans. Officials are hoping operations return to normal before the busy Thanksgiving travel period begins.
Port Authority released a statement Saturday saying,
"Travelers should anticipate continued delays and cancellations at the region's airports throughout the weekend as airlines recover from Friday night's nationwide FAA ground stop. By the end of Friday evening, JFK, LaGuardia, and New York Stewart airports had reported more than 800 cancellations and more than 600 delays.
Airlines are continuing to work through the logistical challenges created by Friday's disruption. Planes were left out of position across the country, and some flight attendants reached their allowable duty limits, requiring carriers to reassign crews and equipment before flights can return to normal schedules.
15% of flights were canceled out of Newark Saturday, 21% at LaGuardia, and 21% at JFK Airport. There were dozens of delays at all three airports.
On Friday evening at LaGuardia, one of the nation's busiest transportation hubs, only a handful of international flights were arriving after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered all flights to stop departing.
Video from the airport around 4:30 p.m. showed aircraft on the runway. About 30 minutes later, roughly a dozen planes were stopped in place as pilots received instructions to return to their gates.
"Nobody is allowed to leave the ground. If you are on the ground, please return to the gate immediately," pilots were told.
Even after flights resumed, some travelers remained stranded or scrambling to adjust their plans.
One passenger trying to reach Belize said the disruption left him frustrated after he missed his flight.
"Unfortunately, we did not make over our flight ... hopefully make it home," he said.
The FAA said it issued the nationwide ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."
Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference Saturday.
"We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related. So we want to be clear that we have a equipment issue, and we're working through what this defective piece of equipment was," Bedford said.
"When we have that root cause analysis complete, we'll share it with you," Bedford said.
He predicted the air travel schedule would fully recover by Sunday.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA does not believe the failure in communications that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday was the result of a cyber attack.
"In at least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they were bringing it over to fiber," Duffy said during a press conference Saturday.
Duffy said this transfer from copper to fiber has been happening in the U.S. for decades, saying virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital.
"Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment, that router that was being replaced as we switched from from copper to fiber, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system. So specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, and what that did was gave us issues with our our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds," Duffy said.
When that happened the airspace was shut down for safety, Duffy said.
"Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online, so we don't believe this was cyber at all. This was an FAA system that didn't meet, didn't meet the moment," Duffy said.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul released a statement saying: "America's airspace ground to a halt yesterday, leaving thousands of flights canceled and travelers stranded across the country. More than 3,500 planes were already in the air as radar and communications systems faltered. We're fortunate no lives were lost.
"From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy's watch.
"Through it all, he's been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency.
"With millions of Americans preparing to travel for the holidays, families deserve answers and confidence in the safety of our skies. Congress must launch a full investigation to determine what went wrong and ensure it never happens again.
"Sean Duffy must resign, or President Trump must remove him immediately."
Major airlines have issued travel waivers for affected passengers this weekend.
American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines are waiving change fees through Saturday, with United also waiving fare differences. Southwest Airlines is allowing passengers to rebook at no additional cost through Monday.
Travelers are encouraged to check directly with their airline and review the status of their itinerary before heading to the airport as carriers continue working to minimize delays and cancellations.
The disruption marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned.
Before that, the last nationwide ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO to test Wall Street’s faith in AI as skepticism mounts
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO to test Wall Street’s faith in AI as skepticism mounts
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
There were no rockets decking Wall Street bank lobbies this past week, unlike the spectacle surrounding SpaceX's blockbuster June listing.
Instead, bankers marketing Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) potentially record-breaking initial public offering this week faced an unusually turbulent backdrop as Treasury yields surged and a widespread Microsoft Outlook outage hampered communications, all during — the biggest disruption of all — the sudden ousting of Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang, whose company is among Anthropic's biggest investors and chip suppliers.
At a JPMorgan Chase investor event Friday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei outlined a future in which AI could help make diseases such as cancer and Alzheimer's relics of the past, while devising entirely new markets in scientific research, robotics, and cybersecurity.
"We can have a much more beautiful world ... It sounds starry-eyed. It sounds crazy. I really do believe it," Amodei told JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon.
Yet Amodei struck a more restrained tone about the company's move to go public, saying he hopes the company will "underpromise and overdeliver."
"We're not super fussed on when exactly, what month or what day or what market conditions we go public into," he added.
The comments come as Anthropic seeks a valuation of approximately $1.3 trillion to $1.4 trillion, below the $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion figures investors had contemplated just weeks earlier.
The offering, expected to begin trading on Thursday, Nov. 19, could provide one of the clearest tests yet of investors' appetite for AI at a moment when enthusiasm for the broader trade is showing signs of cracks.
The contrast between Anthropic's lofty ambitions and Amodei's measured approach to the IPO has also been apparent in Wall Street's marketing campaign.
The lobbies of JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, and Goldman Sachs have been decorated to welcome the startup, according to people familiar with the arrangements. But the displays are more subdued than the digital displays and skyscraper illuminations of rocket ships Wall Street bank visitors witnessed during SpaceX's June IPO, or the meteorite exhibit at JPMorgan's Manhattan headquarters.
Banks are nevertheless mounting a substantial effort to attract investors.
At Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the two banks leading the offering, Anthropic executives met with institutional investors earlier this week. Goldman is also planning an event next week for wealth management clients, where the bank's president, John Waldron, is expected to interview Anthropic president Daniela Amodei and CFO Krishna Rao, according to a people familiar with the plans.
The difference in presentation also arrives as investors appear far more discerning about the extraordinary valuations and spending commitments of AI companies.
Thomas Raymond, a founding partner of Callan Family Office, said his firm is seeking an allocation in Anthropic's IPO through Charles Schwab, arguing that the offering is more attractive than SpaceX's blockbuster listing "simply because of the valuation."
Still, Raymond acknowledged that investor enthusiasm has changed since June, and he wouldn't attempt to purchase shares on the open market.
"There's no escaping the fact that the halo isn't as formidable for all things AI now as compared to three or four months ago," he said.
The more restrained marketing campaign may reflect that shift in sentiment, according to Reena Aggarwal, a Georgetown University finance professor who attended JPMorgan's SpaceX investor event.
"Based on what's happened in the markets, it makes sense not to overdo this," Aggarwal said of Anthropic's IPO.
"You don't want to do a huge amount of fanfare, and, you know, if the stock comes out and crashes, that would look very bad for the company and the bankers," she added.
Even with less spectacle, Anthropic's IPO could deliver one of the largest underwriting paydays in Wall Street history.
Evercore ISI analysts estimate Anthropic's IPO will generate approximately $395 million in underwriting fees, compared with the roughly $500 million fee pool from SpaceX's June listing.
Goldman Sachs ( GS ) and Morgan Stanley ( MS ) could each collect approximately $79 million, while JPMorgan, along with Citigroup ( C ), stand to earn roughly $44 million, according to Evercore's projections.
The fees could climb if the offering size increases beyond what Anthropic has estimated. Banks also could reap additional revenue from the trading, securities lending, and wealth management activity that typically follows a blockbuster listing, Evercore added.
