articles.title_orig: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
articles.title_zh: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
articles.content_orig:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.
Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.
It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.
A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal.
The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.
Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.
The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".
It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".
Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law, and the disproportionate level of the fine.
"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate, and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."
Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.
A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

articles.title_orig: Middle East monarchies brace for Trump corruption scrutiny after blue wave
articles.title_zh: Middle East monarchies brace for Trump corruption scrutiny after blue wave
articles.content_orig:
The US elections have opened a new chapter for artificial intelligence investments by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, democratic gains in Congress, potential restrictions on access to advanced chips, and criticism of data center expansion could alter the conditions under which both countries develop their technology projects.
The Gulf’s bid to become a global leader in computing depends largely on American technology. Therefore, political changes in Washington are raising concerns about the supply of semiconductors, partnerships with technology companies, and the construction of large-scale computing facilities.
Added to this is the debate over the electricity and water consumption of data centers in the United States, this situation could favor the expansion of technological infrastructure in the Middle East, although it also leaves the Gulf countries exposed to regulatory decisions from Washington.
The Democratic victory in the midterm elections introduces new elements to the technological relationship between Washington, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. When the party assumes control of Congress in January, it will have greater opportunities to oversee the artificial intelligence industry. Among the issues that could occupy the legislative agenda are international technological alliances, export controls, and access to advanced computing systems.
This concern is also reflected at the state level, with Democratic candidates who support limiting large data centers winning the governorships of Texas and Georgia. Part of this opposition stems from the impact data centers have on local resources, particularly the increased cost of electricity and water consumption, both of which are gaining traction in discussions about approving new projects.
If these restrictions gain strength, some technology companies could find it more difficult to expand their facilities in the United States and consider other markets to develop their infrastructure.
The supply of semiconductors is one of the most sensitive issues for artificial intelligence projects in the Gulf. Building data centers requires advanced processors, servers, and computing power that depends on international manufacturers and suppliers. Angeline Ong, senior technical analyst at IG, points out that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are seeking to position themselves as global computing hubs for AI, however, access to much of the necessary technology remains contingent on decisions made in Washington.
US restrictions on advanced chips therefore represent a factor that could limit the technological autonomy of regional operators. Adding to this situation is a condition that Nvidia has reportedly set for its data center clients worldwide: at least 51 % of its services must be allocated to non-Chinese companies, according to information published by the Financial Times.
The same outlet reported that Oracle canceled a $7 billion chip leasing agreement with the Chinese company Tencent after receiving pressure from Washington. These cases show that the development of infrastructure for artificial intelligence does not depend solely on investment and the availability of equipment, trade relationships and geopolitical decisions can also determine who has access to this technology and under what conditions.
Despite the restrictions, the main artificial intelligence projects in the Gulf maintain agreements with major US companies, in Saudi Arabia, Humain has the backing of the Public Investment Fund and Saudi Aramco, and the company has established alliances with Amazon Web Services Nvidia and Microsoft to develop its technological capabilities.
In the United Arab Emirates, Microsoft invested $1.5 billion in G42, a technology group based in Abu Dhabi. Through its subsidiary Core42, the company develops cloud infrastructure services and computing solutions for artificial intelligence. According to Angeline Ong, the 51% requirement should not pose an immediate problem for Humain or G42/Core42, as both maintain partner networks oriented toward the West.
Sam Winter-Levy of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace also believes the immediate impact on G42 and Core42 would be limited. However, their current US authorizations expire in April 2027, unless renewed or replaced. This date adds pressure for both companies to maintain operations within the conditions set by Washington. This is compounded by existing delays in deliveries of approved advanced chips due to regulatory hurdles and concerns about potential Chinese access to this technology.
The Humain case presents another element that deserves attention. The company has used technology from MiniMax, a Chinese developer of artificial intelligence models. For now, it is unclear whether the use of Chinese models to provide services to clients in other countries would count toward the limit set by Nvidia.
Winter-Levy explains that Gulf companies have more freedom to decide which AI models to develop or use than to choose the infrastructure needed to run them. The difference is significant. The models are systems trained to perform specific tasks, while their operation depends on a physical infrastructure made up of chips, servers, and specialized equipment.
This means that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates can explore different alternatives for developing their artificial intelligence models, but they have fewer options when they need access to next-generation processors. In this context, diversifying semiconductor suppliers and developing their own manufacturing capabilities are among the alternatives for reducing technological dependence.
The difficulties in expanding large IT facilities within the United States could also benefit the Middle East. Neil Quilliam, a specialist on the region at Chatham House, points out that Gulf governments can more easily offer land, energy supplies, and favorable regulatory conditions than some US jurisdictions.
This environment could prove attractive to technology companies that need to expand their processing capacity and are looking for new locations for their data centers. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates thus have the opportunity to attract new investment and consolidate their digital infrastructures.
However, having available land and energy does not equate to technological independence. Access to advanced semiconductors and the conditions for their use still depend on decisions made outside the region. Quilliam warns that facilitating access to US chips does not mean Washington will relinquish control over their use. The fundamental question remains: who can use this technology and who reaps the benefits of its development?
The new political balance in the United States could expand oversight of international technology agreements. Democrats will have the power to investigate partnerships, hold hearings, and promote measures related to data centers and export controls. However, a breakdown in cooperation with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates is not an inevitable scenario.
Quilliam believes there is bipartisan support for keeping Gulf countries within the US technology ecosystem, rather than favoring closer ties with Chinese suppliers. The extent of any potential restrictions will depend on the decisions Washington makes and the conditions it sets for the supply and use of advanced technology Saudi Arabia and for the United Arab Emirates, the challenge lies in expanding their artificial intelligence capabilities without relying excessively on external regulatory changes.
The expansion of data centers can strengthen their presence in the global digital economy, but access to semiconductors will remain crucial for the development of their technology projects.

articles.title_orig: Why homeowners who go electric have a secret advantage
articles.title_zh: Why homeowners who go electric have a secret advantage
articles.content_orig:
Illustrative photo. Source: Julian Herzog ( Website ) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.
About 6% of U.S. households with at least one vehicle owned an all-electric or plug-in hybrid in 2025, the first year the Census Bureau asked about EV ownership.
EV ownership is most concentrated in the West and major metropolitan areas, according to an Axios analysis of newly released Census Bureau data.
This is reported by Axios .
Where EVs are taking hold will shape who benefits first from electric transportation, where charging networks expand and how quickly the country’s auto market shifts away from gas-powered cars.
California had the highest share of households with an all-electric or plug-in hybrid vehicle in 2025, at 15% - more than double the national rate. Washington, at 9.6%, and Hawaii, at 9.1%, followed, then Nevada at 8.8% and Vermont at 8.1%. North Dakota (1.4%), Wyoming (1.7%) and Louisiana (1.8%) were among the states with the lowest shares.
California’s lead reflects decades of policies encouraging EV purchases and requiring automakers to offer electric models. The state began adopting zero-emission vehicle requirements in 1990. In 2025, California accounted for nearly 30% of U.S. zero-emission passenger vehicle sales, despite having 12% of the nation’s population.
EV ownership was especially concentrated in major metropolitan areas. In the Austin metro area, the share was 9.3%, more than double Texas’s statewide rate of 4.5%. San Francisco’s share was 20%, a high figure in California.
Research has linked higher EV adoption around population centers to household income. Another study found that establishing charging infrastructure boosts adoption, particularly in higher-income areas.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
articles.title_zh: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
articles.content_orig:
Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang."
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker.
Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing , with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June.
The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress , who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence.
"But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday amid multiple affair allegations, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang , who also worked with Nvidia customer Megaspeed . The Singapore-based company is being investigated by the Justice Department for possibly redirecting some of its supply of Nvidia's restricted artificial intelligence chips to China.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X Friday that he signed a petition asking to reinstate Huang. A petition circulating online called "Stand with Jensen" claims to have more than 100,000 signatures, including more than 5,000 current Nvidia employees.
Musk said on X Saturday that without Huang, some "critical deals will be lost."
Another letter sent Friday called on U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee.
Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 about whether the Commerce Department is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips," according to the letter. Huang has also been asked to testify .
The Commerce Department originally launched an investigation into Megaspeed that was moved to the Justice Department in 2025 after Nvidia's lawyer contacted a senior Commerce official, according to The New York Times.
President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit China on Thursday, but doesn't plan to raise Nvidia and the suspected spy affair during his meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping , according to U.S. officials. Musk is expected to join Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

articles.title_orig: Pope laments violence enveloping Peru as he ministers in his former diocese
articles.title_zh: Pope laments violence enveloping Peru as he ministers in his former diocese
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has called for an end to the violence gripping Peru, urging people not to respond to injustice with brutality, as he visited communities he once served as bishop.
“We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters, he said, speaking at his former cathedral in Chiclayo.
Peru’s homicide rate has nearly doubled over the past five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people. Reported extortion cases rose from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025, according to official figures cited by The Associated Press.
Security was a top concern for Peruvians in the last election. Conservative President Keiko Fujimori took office in July after promising to tackle crime. She has since declared states of emergency, including in Lima in August, then in September in prisons holding inmates linked to criminal organisations.
She has also pursued closer ties with Washington, bringing Peru into the ‘Shield of the Americas,’ a US-led regional coalition formed to carry out joint military operations against drug cartels.
Later on Saturday, in the Andean town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba with a population of about 6,000, about 20,000 people came to an outdoor Mass, where Leo also addressed violence in society.
“Selfishness, injustice and evil are not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong, by making our pleas with determination and working diligently to bring about the necessary changes,” said the leader of the Roman Catholic church.
He also drew attention to the suffering of rural communities he used to serve, where migration and declining birth rates are emptying villages.
“Let us think, for example, of the suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future for themselves and their families in the great coastal cities,” he said.
Originally from Chicago in the United States and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo arrived in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba by helicopter and was welcomed by a local band singing “Pope Leo, welcome home.”
He’d made the journey to the remote area many times before during his time as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, driving himself along winding mountain roads in a pick-up truck.
The pope, who holds both US and Peruvian citizenship, spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop.

articles.title_orig: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
articles.title_zh: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
articles.content_orig:
Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown a few weeks ago.
Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.
The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.
Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”
The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.
That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.
The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.
We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.
When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.
However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.
Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.
Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.
Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026.
But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.
Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August 2026.
The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.
Ollie launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard.
Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie was that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aimed to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It kept track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then delivered relevant information to users through text.
However, the app faced a very common challenge: keeping up with heavyweights like Muse and Instinct. Co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon revealed the app would shut down on November 6, citing difficulties like being unable to stand out, failing to grow, and not raising enough capital.
Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.
Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.
Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.
Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 .
The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.
But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.
The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.
However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.
The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.

articles.title_orig: With shifting Iran rhetoric following US elections, Trump leaves Mideast in limbo about path ahead
articles.title_zh: With shifting Iran rhetoric following US elections, Trump leaves Mideast in limbo about path ahead
articles.content_orig:
The Islamic Republic will keep pursuing a nuclear weapon as long as it remains in power, and Washington should keep up military, economic and covert pressure even while it talks to Tehran, Roger Zakheim, director of the Ronald Reagan Institute, told Iran International.
Speaking on Veterans Day, Zakheim said President Donald Trump had set “the first principle” right by vowing to stop Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, a promise he said Trump had made more than 90 times.
“My own view is that as long as this regime is in place, it will pursue a nuclear weapon,” he said. “So if he’s going to prevent the nuclear program, the regime will have to change as well.”
The interview came as Qatar stepped up its mediation. Its foreign ministry said on Tuesday that talks had made progress and that both sides had spoken positively about a diplomatic solution, a day after Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, met Trump at the White House. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, called reports of negotiations or a meeting in Qatar “a pure lie.”
Zakheim, author of a new book on Reagan’s doctrine of peace through strength, said he had no objection to diplomacy, pointing to Reagan’s talks with Mikhail Gorbachev, as long as the pressure continues.
“I’m fine with talks to probe, to explore, to push, as long as we’re squeezing them at the same time: the blockade, the covert operation, the military presence, the ability to carry out a military operation at any moment,” he said. “If it’s diplomacy and everything else stops, I’d be very concerned.”
The US naval blockade of Iranian ports, first imposed in April, remains in place alongside a Treasury sanctions campaign the administration calls Economic Fury. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in Paris on Tuesday that the economic campaign was “so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations.”
Zakheim called the memorandum of understanding reached in June “a very flawed agreement.” Any new deal would need verification involving the United States, “not some third party we can’t trust or don’t know,” he said, and should be “ripped up” if Iran failed to comply.
The June 17 memorandum declared an end to military operations and set a 60-day window for a final deal on Iran’s nuclear program and sanctions. It soon unraveled over control of the Strait of Hormuz, and the deadline passed in August without an agreement.
“They’re just talking about talking,” Zakheim said.
Zakheim gave Trump high marks for Operation Midnight Hammer, the June 2025 US strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, and for Operation Epic Fury, the US-Israeli campaign launched on February 28 that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
“The decapitation, the attacks on the nuclear sites, taking out both the ballistic and cruise missile sites, has made this regime weaker,” he said.
But voters had soured on the war, he said, because the president “didn’t win decisively and got stuck in 140 days of diplomacy with a regime that will never compromise.”
He said he hoped a “very consequential covert program” was under way, with Washington backing those who want to replace the Islamic Republic. “We’ve never had an opportunity like the one we have right now to support the people in Iran who are freedom-loving,” he said, adding that Iran’s borders were “more porous than ever” and its skies open.
“It’s an unnatural regime that oppresses its people,” he said.
Iran executed at least 691 people in the first ten months of 2026, including 36 protesters, according to Norway-based Iran Human Rights, which recorded at least 77 executions in October alone.
No one was calling for US troops on the ground, Zakheim said, but Washington must be ready to strike again if Tehran rebuilds its nuclear or ballistic missile programs.
“After Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury, I felt it was the beginning of the end of this regime, and I still stand by that,” he said.
Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, with anger over the war’s part in pushing up the cost of living helping drive the result, according to Reuters. They also plan to cut Trump’s $1.5 trillion defense budget request, Military.com reported. Zakheim said the president was right to seek it.
The Constitution gives the president, as commander in chief, authority over military and foreign affairs that Congress does not share, Zakheim said, and presidents often turn to foreign policy after midterm losses “because it’s the one thing they can control.” Congress holds the power to declare war and to fund the military.
He warned against a “new generation of détente advocates” and what he called “full-on declinists,” some of whom won seats in the midterms.
“They believe that if only America would retreat from the world and leave, the Iranians would be just fine,” he said. “There’s no evidence of that in the history since 1979.”
He traced Washington’s experience with the Islamic Republic to the 444-day hostage crisis, which ended as Reagan was sworn in in January 1981, and the 1983 bombing of the US Marine barracks in Beirut, which he described as America’s first encounter with Hezbollah.
“You don’t have to look far back to find the number of times this regime has murdered Americans,” he said
The service, the Établissement français du sang (EFS), said in a written reply that a judicial investigation was under way and that it could not comment on it or give details.
The attack took place on the night of November 1 to 2. Hackers took over the control systems of cold rooms at three regional centers and changed their temperature and defrost settings, the EFS said earlier.
Some units were reset from about minus 30 degrees Celsius to 110 degrees, the French weekly Le Canard enchaîné reported. That was the setting, not the temperature the blood products reached.
Alarms and an on-call technician caught the problem, and the products were moved to other sites or otherwise secured, the EFS said. No samples or blood products were lost. The service has not said when the attack was detected, how long the transfer took, or how the stocks were moved.
The attack came the same night that supermarkets in at least nine European countries, including Belgium and Luxembourg, reported suspected cyberattacks that sent fridge and freezer temperatures soaring.
The Paris prosecutor’s office has not yet linked the attack on the blood service to the supermarket cases and said its investigation is continuing, Agence France-Presse reported.
On October 11 and 12, hackers took control of refrigeration systems at about 700 supermarkets and other businesses across France, letting fridges and freezers warm up. Some stores had to throw out their entire stock of fresh and frozen food, and officials said the attacks caused heavy losses and, at some sites, fires.
A joint report by French intelligence and cybersecurity agencies named Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit of the Revolutionary Guards, as responsible, and said it worked behind front groups posing as independent hacker collectives. Paris prosecutors have requested international arrest warrants for suspects.
Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot summoned Iran’s ambassador and said France would seek European Union sanctions against those responsible. France was weighing further measures, he said, including some it might never make public.
Armenia’s parliament approved the agreement on October 28. Since then, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader has threatened Yerevan, and state-run media have urged Tehran to stop the project.
The Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) is designed to link Azerbaijan to its exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenia’s southern Syunik province. Syunik borders Iran’s East Azarbaijan province and carries Iran’s only direct land connection to Armenia, and through it to the rest of the Caucasus.

articles.title_orig: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
articles.title_zh: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of people have joined a protest in Edinburgh against the building of large-scale AI data centres.
Demonstrators with placards - and some dressed in costume - assembled at the top of the Royal Mile before marching towards the Scottish Parliament.
The event comes at a time of widespread debate about the environmental impact of data centres and is part of a wave of protests across Europe.
The Scottish government will soon publish new planning guidance on data centres and said it was developing a strategy to maximise the "public benefit".
Innovation Minister Alyn Smith recently said data centres were "the whisky bonds of the AI sector".
However protesters made it clear they disagree - carrying slogans such as "AI data centres threaten humanity" and "AI data centres: costing the Earth".
Some attended to voice their opposition to plans for data centres in particular communities - including Cockenzie, East Lothian, and Larbert, Falkirk.
Kim Cairns, a campaigner for 'Say No To Chapelcross AI Data Centre', told BBC Scotland News her community was worried about noise, road closures and access problems during the construction phase.
She was also concerned about the noise the centre would generate when it was operational.
Kim said: "It's not going to enrich anybody's lives. For Chapelcross it's the sheer size of it, the amount of electricity it's going to need.
"At the moment it's green fields with sheep and cows in it. It's going to be a monstrosity on the environment.
"The air pollution, the light pollution - it's just not needed."
AI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.
Meanwhile, Scotland's data centre debate centres around the scale and impact of the sites themselves.
At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie, North Lanarkshire, which has a capacity for 12MW.
But if one planned for Chapelcross, Dumfries and Galloway, goes ahead it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world.
The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies.
The innovation minister previously told BBC Scotland some of the discourse around the subject was "wild".
Smith said: "You'd think there wasn't a planning system at all.
"Comparing a really bad data centre in the middle of the Utah desert doesn't track through to what we're going to have in Scotland."
Friends of the Earth campaigner Kim Pratt believes the people of Scotland should have the final say on the building of data centres.
She said: "The way that these data centres are being proposed is going to make a lot of profit for big tech companies but they're going to have huge impacts for people in Scotland.
"These developments are so massive they're going to have national-level impacts -they're energy hungry developments.
"There would be a massive increase in our energy bills but also in terms of climate impact as well.
"The Scottish government is only taking a few months to consider these impacts - and these developments are so new, we don't know what all the impacts will be."
The Scottish government confirmed it would publish new planning guidance on data centres before the end of the year and was "developing a strategic approach to maximising the public benefit from data centres located in Scotland".
A spokesperson added: "Planning authorities are also now required to notify ministers of new data centre applications, with a new planning direction also mandating an Environmental Impact Assessment to be submitted during planning for all new data centres with a power capacity exceeding 50 megawatts."

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin plan unprecedented joint meeting on APEC sidelines, White House and Kremlin say
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin plan unprecedented joint meeting on APEC sidelines, White House and Kremlin say
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump will meet jointly next week with China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the White House said Friday, a first-ever trilateral sit-down between the leaders of the three countries.
The meeting, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, will focus on nuclear non-proliferation, a topic Trump has said he believes could yield a new agreement between the world’s biggest nuclear-armed states.
“The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesman, told reporters.
The Kremlin says that the meeting will take place on November 19 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, but there has been no confirmation yet from China.
While a trilateral convention taking this exact formation is unprecedented, separately the leaders have a wealth of history.
Since becoming president in 2013, Xi has met with Putin dozens of times. The pair have built a close alliance, bound by ties that run deep between their nations.
China has claimed neutrality in the war and sought to position itself as a potential peace broker. But NATO allies believe it has been instrumental in Russia’s effort to defeat Ukraine, providing Moscow with equipment to support weapon assembly, and contributing technology and imagery.
Trump and Putin have convened in-person on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in 2025. The two leaders’ relationship has, at times, been tumultuous, but it appears to have strengthened in recent months.
Trump faced a barrage of domestic criticism in October when he suspended fuel export sanctions on Russia for at least six months, allowing Putin to release diesel into the global energy market at a time when US fuel prices were skyrocketing.
A bipartisan group of lawmakers accused Trump of defying a federal law designed to crack down on Russia and stifle its economy amid its war on Ukraine.
The last nuclear arms treaty between the US and Russia expired in February.
China, meanwhile, has been rapidly building its nuclear arsenal.
Officials downplayed the prospect of striking a new deal on nuclear matters, suggesting instead the talks would be a starting point.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior US official said. “I would characterize this as the entry point, the first conversation, certainly at the leader level, between these countries.”
“So this is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward,” the official went on.
While officials said the three leaders also planned to discuss Iran, it is unclear if they intend to discuss Russia’s near-five-year-old conflict with Ukraine.
Back in October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky voiced concern that a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin might lead to dealmaking about the future of Ukraine without consulting Kyiv.
“We really don’t want this to turn into ‘Yalta 2, 3, 4,’ with a redistribution of influence,” Zelensky told journalists last month, drawing a comparison with the 1945 Yalta Conference in Crimea at which the Allied powers effectively redrew the global map in the aftermath of World War Two.
A senior US official said Elon Musk was expected to go on the trip with Trump, among others, though he is not expected to attend the trilateral meeting.

articles.title_orig: Brain Implants Give A.L.S. Patients the Voice to Speak and Sing
articles.title_zh: Brain Implants Give A.L.S. Patients the Voice to Speak and Sing
articles.content_orig:
Implanted Brain-Computer Interfaces Help Paralyzed Clinical Trial Participants Restore Expressive Communication
Advancements in brain-computer interfaces are helping restore communication in clinical trial participants who have lost the ability to speak or make voluntary movements, according to new research findings scheduled for presentation at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience. Emerging clinical trials evaluating these neural devices indicate that experimental systems can translate recorded brain signals into spoken and written language, moving the technology closer to real-world applications. The scientific meeting, held in Washington, D.C., serves as the world’s largest source of emerging news about brain science and health, highlighting investigations supported by national funding agencies such as the National Institutes of Health alongside private funding organizations.
Brain-computer interfaces operate by recording an individual’s brain signals and translating those neural patterns into actionable commands designed to control computers, prosthetic limbs, or other external devices. Although the technology remains largely experimental at this stage of development, researchers observe that it demonstrates notable promise for restoring essential daily functions that patients have lost as a consequence of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, commonly known as Lou Gehrig’s disease, as well as stroke and other severe neurological disorders. Beyond providing direct assistive utility, the clinical trials involving people with paralysis are also deepening the scientific community’s understanding of how the human brain produces and coordinates speech.
Reflecting the growing clinical promise and technical progress of neural decoding platforms, projections indicate that the global brain-computer interface market will increase from 1.7 billion dollars in 2022 to 6.2 billion dollars by 2030.
Among the specific clinical investigations highlighted at the meeting, researcher Maitreyee Wairagkar of the University of California, Davis, reported that an experimental brain-computer interface utilized a synthetic voice designed to capture pitch variations to facilitate expressive communication for paralyzed patients. By incorporating subtle variations in vocal pitch into the synthesized output, the system improved listener comprehension during conversational exchanges. Furthermore, the pitch-capturing capabilities of the interface proved sufficiently nuanced to enable a participating patient to sing, demonstrating that neural decoding can extend beyond basic lexical content to convey melodic and expressive qualities of human speech.
A distinct clinical evaluation led by Daniel Rubin at Massachusetts General Hospital demonstrated sustained communication capabilities in an individual experiencing a completely locked-in state. In this study, the participant achieved independent communication for more than a year by utilizing a brain-computer interface engineered to decode intended movement directly from recorded brain activity.
Addressing the practical portability and everyday accessibility of neural communication tools, research led by Chethan Pandarinath of the Georgia Institute of Technology and Emory University introduced a portable brain-to-text interface. This system provides accurate, efficient, and reliable decoding of recorded brain activity directly into written words, operating successfully even on consumer hardware such as an iPhone.
Evaluating the broader significance of these collective presentations, event moderator Cynthia Chestek, a biomedical engineer at the University of Michigan who investigates implantable brain-computer interfaces for the neural control of prosthetic limbs and other assistive technologies, emphasized the profound implications of the research. Chestek stated that the ability to decode and convert brain activity into spoken or written words possesses life-changing potential for people living with paralysis. She observed that the work presented at the conference brings brain-to-voice and brain-to-text technologies substantially closer to reaching people outside of clinical trials, which she described as an extremely exciting development for the field.

articles.title_orig: Live updates: SpaceX Starship soars in orbit, still aiming for ship catch in unprecedented test flight
articles.title_zh: Live updates: SpaceX Starship soars in orbit, still aiming for ship catch in unprecedented test flight
articles.content_orig:
In a key test flight on Friday, SpaceX tried but failed to recover both stages of its massive Starship rocket.
The rocket lifted off from the company's South Texas launch facility at 4:47 p.m. local time, or 5:47 p.m. ET. SpaceX had to abort its plans to catch and reuse the booster, instead diverting it to splash into the Gulf of Mexico, where it burst into flames.
Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship mission to date, was the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the booster and upper stage, or spacecraft portion, of the massive rocket.
Earlier on Friday, SpaceX obtained authorization from the Federal Aviation Administration. Hours later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after reporting communication problems affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers. The SpaceX license wasn't effected by the flight stoppage, a spokesperson for the FAA told CNBC.
The upper stage of the Starship continued its trajectory into orbit after the company failed to catch and salvage the booster. The rocket is expected to fly around the Earth fourteen times in total. If successful, SpaceX will land the upper stage back at its Starbase facility on Saturday.
Starship's success is critical to SpaceX and its ambitions to eventually lift cargo and people to the surface of the Moon and Mars. In the near-term, SpaceX needs to send more satellites into orbit to expands its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center.
The company's constellation already includes over 11,000 active satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket has the capacity to carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, the company has said, representing about 20 times the capacity of earlier Falcon 9 rockets.
In the previous Starship test flight, the company released 26 v3 satellites, and released another 26 in the Friday test flight, with the goal of "Starlink becoming 51% of the internet," SpaceX said in a post on X.
When it comes to launches, "SpaceX is likely a full decade ahead of peers on this front," William Blair analysts wrote in a note out on Friday. "Even if tonight's catch is unsuccessful, a delay by a few months is not that consequential."
Meanwhile, SpaceX is facing fresh criticism over restrictions imposed on its Starshield satellite internet service in Ukraine. Starshield is built on Starlink technology and is the military-tier of SpaceX's satellite internet service.
Earlier this week, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country's military forces had experienced limits on Starshield without warning again, harming their ability to defend against Russia's ongoing aerial attacks. Similar limits on Starshield in Ukraine were temporarily imposed last month .
Some U.S. senators have condemned the restrictions, and urged Congress to investigate SpaceX .

articles.title_orig: Pope’s visit to hub of Afro-Peruvian community casts spotlight on African slave trade to Peru
articles.title_zh: Pope’s visit to hub of Afro-Peruvian community casts spotlight on African slave trade to Peru
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has called for an end to the violence gripping Peru, urging people not to respond to injustice with brutality, as he visited communities he once served as bishop.
“We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters, he said, speaking at his former cathedral in Chiclayo.
Peru’s homicide rate has nearly doubled over the past five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people. Reported extortion cases rose from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025, according to official figures cited by The Associated Press.
Security was a top concern for Peruvians in the last election. Conservative President Keiko Fujimori took office in July after promising to tackle crime. She has since declared states of emergency, including in Lima in August, then in September in prisons holding inmates linked to criminal organisations.
She has also pursued closer ties with Washington, bringing Peru into the ‘Shield of the Americas,’ a US-led regional coalition formed to carry out joint military operations against drug cartels.
Later on Saturday, in the Andean town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba with a population of about 6,000, about 20,000 people came to an outdoor Mass, where Leo also addressed violence in society.
“Selfishness, injustice and evil are not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong, by making our pleas with determination and working diligently to bring about the necessary changes,” said the leader of the Roman Catholic church.
He also drew attention to the suffering of rural communities he used to serve, where migration and declining birth rates are emptying villages.
“Let us think, for example, of the suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future for themselves and their families in the great coastal cities,” he said.
Originally from Chicago in the United States and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo arrived in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba by helicopter and was welcomed by a local band singing “Pope Leo, welcome home.”
He’d made the journey to the remote area many times before during his time as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, driving himself along winding mountain roads in a pick-up truck.
The pope, who holds both US and Peruvian citizenship, spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop.

articles.title_orig: AT&T begins shutting down landline services in Middle Tennessee this weekend, here's what to know
articles.title_zh: AT&T begins shutting down landline services in Middle Tennessee this weekend, here's what to know
articles.content_orig:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WTVF) — Starting this Sunday, AT&T will begin shutting down landline services across several Middle Tennessee communities after receiving permission from the Federal Communications Commission.
While the change may not affect everyone directly, experts say homeowners and business owners should know a few key things before the service disappears.
You're talking about fax lines, security lines, elevator lines — especially when it comes to condos, townhomes, business centers, medical plazas. That's where you're going to see the vast majority of them," said Stephen Burton from One Call Technology in Franklin.
The team at One Call Technology is already helping businesses prepare for the day their phone provider pulls the plug — a day that is quickly approaching.
"Different carriers are shutting off at different times, but people don't think it applies to them necessarily yet," said Burton.
An AT&T filing with the FCC shows the company plans to begin discontinuing service this weekend from dozens of wire centers across Tennessee. AT&T has until 2029 to complete the full transition.
For anyone with safety systems like fire alarms and emergency phones, experts say it's time to act now—before those systems stop working.
Navigating the changes does not have to be overwhelming.
"Reach out to a company. There are a lot in the Middle Tennessee area that you can talk with who are well aware of what's going on and can hold your hand and walk you through it," said Burton.
Something else to keep an eye on is what you're paying for older services going forward.
With pricing regulations no longer in place, some customers have seen the cost of their copper-based services climb dramatically.

articles.title_orig: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
articles.title_zh: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
articles.content_orig:
A masked demonstrator prepares to throw a Molotov cocktail as police use a water cannon to disperse students protesting education policies, rising living costs and reduced sentences for people convicted of sexual offenses against minors in Santiago, Chile, Nov. 5, 2026. Esteban Felix/AP hide caption
SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.
José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.
It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.
But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.
"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.
"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.
Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.
Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.
Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.
But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.
In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.
Trucks are parked along a road as drivers protest rising fuel prices and operating costs on the outskirts of Santiago, Chile, Nov. 12, 2026. Esteban Felix/AP hide caption
This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.
On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.
It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.
Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.
In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll.
At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.
"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.
Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.
To the contrary, his budget proposal is making its way through Congress, with the government seeking cuts to education, culture, science and a host of social programs.

articles.title_orig: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
articles.title_zh: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
articles.content_orig:
PM accuses Tories of burning ‘all our bridges’ and says deal he is pursuing with EU will ‘get food prices down’
Andy Burnham has said the UK has “lost more than we gained” since leaving the EU, the prime minister’s latest in a string of comments criticising Brexit.
Outlining his desire to form closer ties with Brussels, Burnham accused the Conservative party of having “burned all our bridges” with the bloc after Brexit and said a new deal he hopes to secure with the EU next week will “get food prices down” and put more money in the pockets of British exporters.
The prime minister is due to meet European leaders at a summit next week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. He will also “explore options” for a different long-term relationship with Brussels.
Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham said: “We need to be willing to take difficult decisions to get the cost of living down.
“It’s why, in a few days’ time, I will head to the next UK-EU summit and I will be working hard as we move towards it to get to a new deal on food and farming between the UK and the EU. Why am I doing that? Because I want to help Welsh businesses.
The prime minister added: “I think we’ve lost more than we’ve gained over the last 10 years, and, actually, I think the Conservatives gave Britain a harsher and harder Brexit than people thought they were getting when they voted in 2016, because they burned all of our bridges in the aftermath, with the EU, and so I’m going to lead as prime minister on this issue, and I’m going to go and try and get the best deal I can for Wales, for those here who could benefit, Welsh farmers, exporters of Welsh shellfish and Welsh lamb.”
Burnham has recently said he is open to rejoining the single market, customs union or to “go all the way” by rejoining the EU, but on Saturday he said voters would ultimately be “the boss” of any changes.
He reiterated his commitment to Labour’s manifesto “red lines” – which rule out returning to the customs union, single market or free movement. “People working together in unions, trade unions, but also unions of nations, and that’s what makes us who we are,” he told the conference.
“And, yes, working with the European Union , as I said, but at the same time respecting the red lines in our manifesto and respecting the referendum, the referendum result. So, that’s the spirit, everybody, that I will take forward.”
The government has already made several announcements that would tie the UK closer to Brussels. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported that the UK was prepared to spend up to £450m a year to give EU students discounted university tuition fees, if Brussels allowed Britain access to the Made in Europe industrial programme.
Earlier this week, Hamish Falconer, the cabinet minister in charge of EU talks, said Britain was willing to discuss paying towards infrastructure schemes in poorer parts of the EU in return for access to the European electricity market.
after newsletter promotion
Despite Burnham’s recent pro-EU comments, senior figures in Brussels have said they want to see the UK begin to start paying for access to the European schemes it says it wants access to.
The EU’s former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier told the BBC last week: “There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market.”
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and António Costa, who leads the European Council, will meet Burnham on 20 November in Brussels for a summit where deals on food and drink, carbon emissions and youth exchange could be signed.
Barnier said the UK could not rejoin the single market “à la carte”, when speaking to the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg last Sunday, adding: “I said very, very often during these negotiations, the Brexit, there is no cherrypicking.”

articles.title_orig: Jim Cramer has a strong take on Nvidia’s next chapter
articles.title_zh: Jim Cramer has a strong take on Nvidia’s next chapter
articles.content_orig:
CNBC's Jim Cramer criticized former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday for putting the chipmaker's future at risk.
"Did he betray you, the shareholders?" Cramer asked. "Yes. End of story."
Huang resigned Thursday morning following reports of an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Hours later, Reuters reported that he had an "intimate relationship" with a second employee. These revelations came days after Huang admitted to an affair with an executive at a Singapore-based cloud computing company whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China. Longtime CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO of Nvidia. Cramer said Huang's departure was necessary to protect Nvidia from further fallout.
Shares ended Thursday down more than 4%, but at its lows of the morning, the stock was off over 14%. The decline in Thursday's session brings Nvidia's losses this year to 12%.
While questions remain about what comes next for the AI chipmaker, Cramer argued that Nvidia's future extends beyond the executive who helped build it into one of the world's most valuable companies. "There won't be a better Nvidia, just a different one [without Huang]," Cramer said, envisioning a company that is better organized and more disciplined about its investments.
Under Huang, Nvidia built an extensive equity investment portfolio that included a $5 billion investment in Intel in 2025 and a $2 billion investment in AI cloud provider CoreWeave earlier this year. The investments, and many others, were part of Huang's strategy to strengthen Nvidia's position across the AI industry.
During the CNBC Investing Club's Morning Meeting livestream Thursday, Cramer recalled urging Kress to reduce the company's stakes in Intel and CoreWeave, only to be told that Huang preferred to maintain them. Cramer suggested that new leadership could take a more disciplined approach to capital allocation, potentially cashing in on some of those investments and returning the proceeds to shareholders through even bigger stock buybacks.
Cramer expressed confidence in Kress, praising her deep understanding of Nvidia's operations and financials. He argued that the longtime finance chief is well positioned to provide stability as the company navigates the investigations surrounding Huang, which stretch from the boardroom to Washington, D.C.
Nvidia didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment on Cramer's remarks. Heller, the crisis PR firm Huang reportedly hired as early as last year, did not respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Going forward, Nvidia's underlying business remains strong, Cramer said, pointing to its substantial cash reserves and expectations for a robust earnings report Tuesday evening. But he cautioned that even strong quarterly results might not be enough to reassure investors during this time of lingering uncertainty.
Investigations into Huang's conduct and possible violations of U.S. chip export restrictions could result in sanctions that hurt Nvidia's international business. Meanwhile, competitors, including Advanced Micro Devices , are making progress with their own AI chips, potentially threatening Nvidia's market dominance. AMD shares surged almost 6% on Thursday, extending their winning streak to five straight sessions.
Those risks have prompted Cramer to take a more cautious approach to Nvidia stock , particularly after the substantial gains shares have delivered over the years for Cramer's Charitable Trust , the portfolio of 32 stocks managed by the Club. On Tuesday, as Huang's future at Nvidia looked more and more in doubt, the Club downgraded Nvidia to a hold-equivalent rating.
"Don't ever turn a successful investment into an unsuccessful trade," he said, urging longtime shareholders sitting on big gains to consider taking some profits. "You don't want to give up all of your gains if the stock falls further. It fell further today after many of the analysts jumped ship and downgraded the stock from buy to hold. There could be more ahead."
At the same time, Cramer cautioned against giving up on Nvidia altogether, pointing to the company's extensive engineering expertise and multiyear product roadmap as reasons to believe it can continue competing at the forefront of AI without Huang.
The "Mad Money" host also drew parallels to Apple's leadership transition from Steve Jobs to Tim Cook , suggesting that Nvidia could benefit from a similarly capable successor who brings a different management style without sacrificing the company's technological edge.

SpaceX succesfully launched its Starship Flight 15 mission on Friday, Nov. 13 , at 5:47 p.m. EDT (2247 GMT) from Starbase, Texas. Starship Flight 15 will attempt to land its Ship upper stage for the first time, but did abort a landing pad catch of its Super Heavy Booster. It will be the first-ever recovery of an orbital Starship upper stage, if successful. See launch video above and live views from SpaceX .
Follow our Starship Flight 15 coverage here as SpaceX completes its final prelaunch work for the launch, which also deployed 26 new Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.
Flight 15 landing livestream | Flight 15 launch video | SpaceX | Starship
Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon .
Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.
Ship has officially reentered Earth's atmosphere on its planned trip back to Texas' Starbase site for a historic "chopsticks" catch. The effects of our air on the vehicle are obvious; super-hot plasma now surrounds Ship's leading edges as it continues its descent.
All remains on schedule for a catch attempt around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT).
SpaceX just gave us some more information about why the Super Heavy booster aborted its chopsticks-catch try shortly after Starship's Flight 15 launch yesterday (Nov. 13).
"Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," SpaceX's Kate Tice said today (Nov. 14) during the company's Flight 15 webcast (which is ongoing, as Starship's Ship upper stage is currently coming back to Earth for its own catch , a milestone scheduled to occur at around 4:16 p.m. EST, 2116 GMT).
"The team is still investigating the root cause on that," Tice added. "However, booster guidance then detected that it wasn't in the right position as it was flying back, so the booster correctly aborted itself from the tower catch and went for an offshore water divert instead."
Starship 's Ship upper stage just began its descent back toward Earth. At about 3:23 p.m. EST (1823 GMT) today (Nov. 14), the vehicle conducted a 10-second, single-engine deorbit burn that went according to plan.
"Good deorbit burn," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during SpaceX's webcast today. "Starship [is] on its way back through the atmosphere soon."
Ship remains on target to return to SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms at around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT) — about 22.5 hours after it launched from the same pad on Starship's 15th test flight.
Good news, space fans: A "chopsticks" catch attempt of Starship 's Ship upper stage is officially on for this afternoon (Nov. 14).
"Moments ago, the launch team conducted the final planned contingency check for Ship's return to the launch site," SpaceX' s Kate Tice said during a webcast update today. "And, great news: All teams have polled 'go.' That included Stage 2, heat shield, flaps, structures, aero, guidance, navigation and control and, of course, the tower."
If all goes to plan, Ship will return to SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, where it will be snagged by its launch tower's arms at around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT), bringing an end to Starship Flight 15 , which launched on Friday evening (Nov. 13). SpaceX has never tried a chopsticks catch with Ship before, so tune in here at Space.com to see how it goes!
We just got some updated information about Super Heavy's landing abort during Starship Flight 15. SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot initially said that the booster diverted away from a "chopsticks" catch attempt at Starbase on Friday (Nov. 13) due to a guidance, navigation and control (GNC) issue. This morning (Nov. 14), however, he exonerated the GNC system, saying it performed as expected during Super Heavy's return to Earth.
The GNC system "detected that the booster was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch, did an automated abort and then headed out to that offshore splashdown location," Huot said. "The team's still digging into the root cause on how we got there, and so, more to come on that."
You can read our story about Super Heavy's landing abort here .
SpaceX is still planning to catch Starship's Ship upper stage at Starbase today. Everything looks good for that unprecedented attempt, which will occur at around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT), if all goes according to plan. You can watch it live here at Space.com.
We are now 16 hours into SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission , with just over six more hours remaining until the Ship 42 upper stage makes its attempted landing catch back at Starbase.
In an earlier post, I discussed SpaceX's update on how a guidance system issue caused the Super Heavy booster landing abort just after liftoff. You can now read my full story on the Super Heavy landing abort here .
Space.com's Josh Dinner captured the moment the Super Heavy booster triggered its flight termination system to explode in the Gulf of Mexico offshore from Starbase. Check it out.
Until the landing abort, the Starship Super Heavy booster performed as expected during its liftoff and stage separation, delivering its Ship upper stage to the proper position to fire its own engines and reach orbit.
Here's a stunning look at all 33 Super Heavy Raptor engines firing in unison to power the 41-story rocket's ascent into orbit, as seen by Josh.
The next Flight 15 milestone for SpaceX will be a "Final Hawaii Return Check" at the 20-hours, 41-minute mark of the mission. That will be a go/no-go moment when SpaceX decides whether to attempt the Starbase chopsticks landing at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT) for Ship 42, or direct it to a splashdown off the coast of Hawaii.
Our landing livestream will begin at about that check in time, at 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT).
Good morning and happy Saturday, Space Fans! Today is Flight Day 2 for SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight and SpaceX reports that its Ship 42 spacecraft is in good health as we near the 14-hour mark of its 22.5-hour test flight.
About 7 hours into the mission, SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot confirmed that flight controllers gave the go-ahead to forgo an early return window for a splashdown off the coast of Chile and proceed for the full 14-orbit flight. Starship is on track for a landing attempt, its first-ever from orbit, today (Nov. 14) at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT) . Space.com's livestream of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 landing will begin at 2 p.m. EST and you can see it at the top of this page.
"Starship's going to stay in space. We are one step closer to an eventual return to launch site," Huot said in the update. "So that's great news."
Huot also reported that Starship's tile-covered heat shield appears in good shape for today's landing attempt. SpaceX used long-range ground-based cameras and cameras on some of the 26 Starlink satellites the Ship deployed to check its heat shield after liftoff.
"Our heat shield team reviewed all the data we got from our ground tracking cameras, and from those satellite cameras and confirmed the heat shield is in a good posture for a reentry and return to the launch site," Huot said.
