articles.title_orig: Grandmother mistakes medieval gold cross for costume jewelry before learning its five-figure value
articles.title_zh: Grandmother mistakes medieval gold cross for costume jewelry before learning its five-figure value
articles.content_orig:
A grandmother unearthed a medieval gold cross while metal detecting on an island with historic ties to King Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. Now, she's hoping the potentially valuable treasure could have a royal connection.
A grandmother recently discovered a medieval gold cross while metal detecting in a farmer's field — and it could be worth tens of thousands of dollars.
The cross was found by 58-year-old metal detecting hobbyist Shelley Couzins in August, news agency Southwest News Service (SWNS) reported. The discovery was only recently publicized.
Couzins, a grandmother of five who took up metal detecting four years ago, told SWNS she was out with a group on the Isle of Sheppey in Kent in the United Kingdom when, after five hours of searching, she found nothing but "rubbish."
MYSTERIOUS FIND BENEATH FIELD LEADS MAN TO MASSIVE TREASURE HIDDEN FOR CENTURIES
Around lunchtime, her metal detector suddenly began beeping, prompting her to dig roughly 12 inches into the freshly plowed soil.
"It was quite quiet all morning, and then I heard this beep," Couzins recalled.
Shelley Couzins unearthed a medieval gold reliquary cross after spending five hours searching a freshly plowed field in southeastern England. (Shelley Couzins/SWNS)
She soon unearthed a gold cross — but initially dismissed it as costume jewelry.
It wasn't until she returned to the group's main tent that fellow hobbyists told her the cross was made of real gold.
REAL-LIFE EXCALIBUR? MAN ON A HIKE UNCOVERS GOLD SWORD RELIC HIDDEN UNDER TREE
"It is like a metal detectorist's dream ," Couzins told SWNS.
"You only find something like this once in a lifetime."
The medieval gold reliquary cross discovered in England can be opened to hold religious relics, though its finder chose to leave it sealed. (Shelley Couzins/SWNS)
Couzins was searching with a group called Medway History Finders, which has withheld the field's exact location over concerns about illegal treasure hunters.
The cross, which weighs 10.6 grams, was subsequently reported to a Finds Liaison Officer under England's treasure reporting process.
MYSTERY DEEPENS AFTER 2,700-YEAR-OLD BRONZE SWORD EMERGES STANDING UPRIGHT
The grandmother said she was "absolutely gutted" about having to surrender the artifact .
"I like to keep everything I find. I know I will probably never see it again," Couzins said.
"I am happy for it to go to a good home, where it needs to go, instead of sitting in my cupboard."
The artifact was identified as a medieval gold reliquary cross, depicting Jesus' crucifixion on one side and the Virgin Mary holding baby Jesus on the other, according to SWNS.
The cross can also be opened to hold religious relics, though Couzins said she left it sealed for fear of damaging it.
2,000-YEAR-OLD TREASURE DISCOVERED BENEATH FORMER SPORTS FIELD, BREAKING REGIONAL RECORD
The artifact is being assessed by the British Museum, according to SWNS. Its ultimate ownership and value have yet to be determined.
If acquired through the treasure process, the cross would be valued, with any resulting reward expected to be split between Couzins and the landowner.
Shelley Couzins, pictured on the left, said she was disappointed to surrender the medieval gold cross she discovered but hopes the historic artifact will be preserved. (Shelley Couzins/SWNS)
Online estimates have placed the cross's potential value at a minimum of £20,000 (roughly $27,000), though no official valuation has been announced, said SWNS.
Couzins also expressed relief that the delicate artifact had survived the plowing of the field without being destroyed.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
"I really love that I saved it," she said. "If that plough had gone over again, it might have picked that up and broken it in two."
Despite her disappointment at having to give up the cross , Couzins said she hopes it will be preserved.
Couzins, pictured on the right, initially believed the gold cross she discovered in a farmer's field was a piece of costume jewelry. (Shelley Couzins/SWNS)
"I am happy for it to go to a good home, where it needs to go, instead of sitting in my cupboard."
The Isle of Sheppey has historical ties to King Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, who visited Shurland Hall on the island in October 1532, according to Historic England.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
Couzins said she hopes the cross might have a connection to the royal couple, though no evidence has emerged linking the artifact to either figure.
"There are links here to Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn," she told SWNS. "We can't say it belonged to them, but that history makes this find more interesting because there could be a possibility that it is linked."
Fox News Digital reached out to Couzins for additional comment.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The discovery follows other finds of early medieval Christian artifacts across Europe in recent years.
King Henry VIII, seen center, and Anne Boleyn, seen left, visited Shurland Hall on England's Isle of Sheppey in October 1532, centuries before a grandmother discovered a medieval gold cross on the island. (Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty Image)
Last year, a metal detectorist discovered a 1,200-year-old gilded Christian cross in a field in Leeds, England.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A few months later, in Germany, archaeologists reported the discovery of another Christian cross among more than 200 Viking-era artifacts dating back roughly 1,000 years.
Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com .

articles.title_orig: How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
articles.title_zh: How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

Math isn’t my strong suit. I’m a word nerd (and a gear nerd). But REI’s latest sale —a holiday extravaganza that’s overflowing with deals—has me crunching numbers. There are over 3,000 products on offer, with discounts of up to 25 percent off. According to the pytha-gear-eum theorem, that math means I’m allowed to fill up 2.7 cubic meters of garage space with new gear.
All jokes aside, REI’s mega sale runs from November 13th through the 23rd, giving you an ample window to hammer out your holiday shopping—or add some gear to your own garage. To help you sift through this supersized sale, I combed through REI’s labyrinth of clearance shelves to bring you nine deals that I wouldn’t hesitate to scoop up right here, right now.
Mountain Hardwear’s take on the ubiquitous grid fleece, the Summit Grid series offers a balanced blend of everyday coziness and alpine proficiency. In particular, the Summit Big Grid Hoody ( men’s and women’s ) has been my favorite layer this fall. It’s as comfy as my most prized sweatshirts, but way more capable when it comes to hiking, frigid trail runs, you name it. The fit is a bit baggy for the ultralight crowd, but the oversized silhouette is modern and slick. Five stars—a perfect holiday gift for any outdoorsy (or outdoorsy-ish) person on your list. REI Co-op members get 20% off with coupon HOLIDAY2026.
There are certain things I strongly believe you should splurge on. Snowboards, for instance. You get what you pay for there. But other gear categories, like base layers, you can often get away with a more affordable option. REI Co-op base layers fall into the latter category. That said, I’d recommend skipping the synthetics and stepping up to REI’s 100-percent merino base layers . Merino’s a natural fiber with intrinsic warmth and wicking properties, plus antimicrobial magic for hut trips and multi-day ski road trips. Yes, REI’s merino options are pricier than the Co-op synthetics, but they’re also significantly cheaper than pure merino base layers from the competition—especially during REI’s holiday sale.
I’ve relied on Thule RoundTrip snowboard bags on multiple international shred missions over the years, from road trips through British Columbia’s Powder Highway to train-hopping around the Alps. Fat rolling wheels, easy-grab handles, and ample padding and protection make these Thule ski and snowboard bags an easy recommendation, even at full retail. However, all Thule ski and snowboard bags are currently 25 percent off. Skiers will be stoked to note that tester-approved RoundTrip boot bags are similarly on sale. And snowboarders will be stoked to note that they don’t need a boot bag.
The Car Seat Towel is basically just a regular quick-drying Nomadix towel , with a small hood that slips over your car headrest. It doesn’t secure tightly to your car seat like a designated seat cover, but it works well enough on the road. I just put it to the test on a three-week road trip to the Tetons and had no complaints in that department. The real beauty is that it doubles as a proper towel, too, so you can dry off after impromptu swims, surfs, you name it. On that Teton road trip, the Car Seat Towel was a day-saver after the muddiest day of fly-fishing of my life. Apart from the ski socks you’ll find below, this is also the most affordable pick in this article, and a gift that any self-respecting (and rig-respecting) road tripper will dig.
There’s no piece of gear in this article—hell, in the entirety of that 7000+ product REI sale—that I use more than the AeroPress Steel . (Once daily, twice if I’m on deadline, three times if I’m looking longingly at that deadline in my rearview mirror.) If you already have an AeroPress that you know and love, this uses the same plunging pressure to yield a velvety cup of coffee. However, the AeroPress Steel ditches the plastic for a bomber, stainless steel body that I’m pretty sure I could run over with my Subaru. In fact, I just might run it over with my Subaru, for the sake of science, knowing that it’s now on sale for $119 at REI.
I’ve recommended the Smith Squad MAG more times than I can count. (I’m not a math guy, remember?) The lens interchangeability system balances the speed of magnets with the security of a locking mechanism, style is through the roof, and the lenses themselves are high-quality and offer excellent contrast and definition on the hill. If you’re unsure what to nab a skier or snowboarder for the holidays, my advice is always a pair of goggles. Lenses get scratched or lost easily, and any powderhound will appreciate an optical refresh.
If you replaced virtually all of my closet with Roark duds (technical outerwear aside), I’d be quite content. I’d also be quite stylish. And my wife would be quite content, too. Peep the Roark lineup here for suave men’s and women’s adventure wear, all discounted by 25 percent. Or, take a gander at my personal Roark go-to: the Bless Up Trail Shirt . An ultralight travel shirt that’s breathable enough for desert backpacking yet snazzy enough for summer nights on the town, this is a staple for me on any warm-weather trip. It’s also so packable that it would make a killer stocking stuffer!
Whether you’re in the market for a featherweight backpacking bag like the Spark , a lofty quilt like the Ember for fast-and-light alpine missions, or a cozy and wearable sleeping bag like the Trek , Sea to Summit’s got you covered. Well-designed, built to last, and currently on sale for 25 percent off—that’s a combo that’ll help any camper sleep soundly.
Stuffing Smartwool ski socks in a stocking is Inception-level gifting. It’s a sock—in a sock! It’s also an incredibly practical gift that any skier or snowboarder will appreciate immensely when the mercury drops, the powder falls, and the Sock Monster has swallowed up mate after mate, leaving behind a rag-tag collection of singles in the sock drawer. Of course, the sock monster is inevitable, his lust for lint unslakable. Eventually, these Smartwool socks, no matter how smart they really are, will be hunted, measured, and tasted by this Dark Lord of Laundry. Luckily, when that day comes, you’ll have gotten these particular Smartwool ski socks for 25 percent off. And half a pair of socks that you got for a quarter off is still a pretty good deal. But, again, I’m not a math guy.

The iPhone Duo is easily the most impressive device Apple has made thus far, at least since the early years of the iPhone. Not only is it a whole new form factor, it includes things that you straight-up won't find on traditional iPhones. Certainly not the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
But as big a deal as the first foldable iPhone is, 2027 will mark the 20th anniversary of the very first iPhone. Rumor has it that, like the iPhone X in 2017, Apple will celebrate the milestone with an all-new iPhone design . Word has it that this so-called iPhone 20 will feature a curved glass body that makes the phone look like it's made of 100% glass.
But there's guaranteed to be a lot more to the next iPhone than just a fancy design. And if Apple has any sense it should take some of the better parts of the iPhone Duo for the iPhone 20, while also making sure to ignore other aspects of the foldable's design.
You may be thinking, "isn't the iPhone 20 supposed to have an all-glass design? How does titanium fit into it?", and you make a valid point. The titanium used on other iPhones is only present at the surface of the frame, and the internal body is made from much cheaper aluminum.
If the iPhone 20 replaces that metal frame with glass, then there's no space for titanium, right? Yes, but that hinges on the curved all-glass design rumor actually coming true. Glass is not the easiest material to work with, especially when you're trying to do new things. So there's a chance that design may not happen, and if it doesn't Apple needs to bring back that premium material to get that mix of strength and low weight.
Because, let's be honest, the anodized aluminum shell isn't really cutting it right now.
Steve Jobs may have hated the idea of using a stylus with an iPhone, but the iPhone Duo proved that their usefulness isn't just limited to iPads. Sure, the iPhone 20 won't have as much screen space as the iPhone Duo's 7.6-inch inner display, but that doesn't mean we have to be limited to finger-based control.
Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.
Offering Apple Pencil support on iPhones means you get a lot more precision control. Whether you want to draw, write, take notes, and so on. It offers a bunch more versatility to the way you control your iPhone, and in a way that's totally optional. This clearly isn't one of those early smartphones that only worked if you kept hold of a little plastic tip.
In a similar situation, Apple may have insisted that Touch ID is wholly inferior to Face ID , from a security standpoint, but it's nice to have options. The iPhone Duo shows that Apple can add the power button Touch ID to an iPhone, offering a discreet fingerprint scanner away from the front of the phone.
This shouldn't necessarily mean the loss of Face ID, as was the case with iPhone Duo. It would be nice if Apple offered both, and gave users the option of which biometric security option they prefer. Personally, I much prefer Touch ID over Face ID, but some of my colleagues would disagree.
Plus, where security is concerned, no amount of biometric security will make up for a weak passcode.
Split-screen multitasking is not an uncommon feature on modern phones, but it's been totally absent from iPhones until the launch of iPhone Duo — and that needs to change . Admittedly, split-screen multitasking is more troublesome on a phone screen, since there's less space to fit multiple windows. However, that doesn't mean it can't be useful on slab phones.
We've all experienced times when we're using our phone for something, and keep having to move back and forth between different apps. Having the option to multitask means that you could just load those two apps up side by side instead. Saving you the hassle of switching, and avoiding any awkward reloading that the apps might want to do when you return.
Another feature that's so common people don't even think about anymore is the hole punch camera. It's also something Apple seems to have deliberately avoided offering until the release of the iPhone Duo — and it's about time it came to more iPhones.
The obvious problem has always been Face ID hardware. This is why Apple had such large notches for so long, and why it later adopted the Dynamic Island. But we're getting to the stage where most of that hardware has been hidden away, and the iPhone 20 is the perfect time for Apple to push the rest of it under the screen where we can't see it.
If Apple can hide a camera under the Duo's screen, I'm sure it can hide the remainder of Face ID — even if the camera itself isn't ready to be out of sight.
One of the early iPhone 20 rumors was that it would have an uninterrupted display, thanks to the adoption of under-display tech. However, at least one recent rumor has contradicted those claims, and I hope it turns out to be correct. Apple markets the Duo's under-display camera as a "FaceTime camera," meant to be used for video calls rather than selfies. All because the camera quality is not very good compared to traditional selfie cameras.
The camera is hidden under the display by pixels that can effectively be switched off. Combined with a localized area of low pixel density, it allows light through to reach the camera. Sadly there are still obstacles in the way that interfere with that process, even if they're not as easy to see, and that affects the camera's quality. It's why under-display cameras fell out of favor in the first place.
That's fine on a foldable that already has a traditional selfie camera, and the option to shoot selfies with the main cameras. But the iPhone 20 won't have either of those things, and opting for an under-display camera is just going to mean users won't be able to take nice selfies.
We have seen an explosion of wide-shaped foldables this year, seemingly in anticipation of iPhone Fold and for the most part that design change has gone down pretty well. The shorter and wider screens are fairly comfortable to use, and there tends to be less unused space when you're watching a show or move on the foldable screen.
But we've also started seeing some phone companies produce non-foldable devices with wider screens . I've never used one, and I can't comment on how they compare to normal phone dimensions, but this trend is not something Apple should copy.
Apple isn't one for chasing trends, so this isn't likely to happen, but considering wider non-folding phones is still an unproven design, no phone company should be rushing to switch up its entire design language. Least of all a company that only releases six models each year.
The nanotexture display coating has a bunch of benefits for the iPhone Duo, ensuring a glare-free display and minimizing the look of the central crease. However, it also has the added hindrance of reducing the vividness of colors and making the screen look more washed out.

articles.title_orig: ‘GTA 6’ Reveals Jason And Lucia’s Limited Crime Options To Start
articles.title_zh: ‘GTA 6’ Reveals Jason And Lucia’s Limited Crime Options To Start
articles.content_orig:
Rockstar Games recently sat down to give their one-millionth interview about Grand Theft Auto 6. Not really, but it feels like that sometimes. In the interview, they discussed the open-world potential of GTA 6, which releases worldwide next week. They spoke about crime and punishment, how the characters develop alongside one another, and how you can have ’empathy’ this time around.
While talking and playing the game during the interview, Rockstar’s Rob Nelson, who is fast becoming the PR face of GTA 6, explained how the story progresses with Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, the game’s co-protagonists. Like other games in the series, and in games like Red Dead, you start as a relatively small fish in a big pond.
Grand Theft Auto 6 represents the pinnacle of freedom; that much is certain. From what we’ve seen in the trailers released thus far, we’re getting a gargantuan world absolutely brimming with opportunities to explore, enjoy what’s on offer, and yes, wreak a little havoc.
But it’s not all about being a nasty criminal this time around. Rockstar recently confirmed that you can have empathy in this game for the first time in franchise history.
Rob Nelson spoke to The Guardian about the concept of crime in GTA 6, and he laid out the inner workings of the game’s story. As Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, the loved-up dual protagonists of this game, you’re not immediately able to waltz into a high-end jewelry store and make your fortune.
It’s a staggered, tiered system, it sounds like.
The interview context explains how the pair ‘can’t just steal any car or bust their way into a bank’ right out of the gate. Players will start by hotwiring low-end vehicles and picking ‘basic locks’, robbing convenience stores and gas stations before working their way up to the bigger, heftier targets.
We’ve already heard how certain cars will provide blockers to being stolen, boasting intelligent anti-theft systems, alarms, trackers, and immobilizers. We know how some store clerks will fight back, how passers-by will identify you to the police, and how people will record things on their phones, giving you a digital footprint.
It’s a fairly natural thing to assume that we wouldn’t start GTA 6 as master criminals, but in the trailers that we’ve seen thus far, we know we’re working towards that . We’ve seen Jason and Lucia robbing some pretty intense locations, decked out in body armor and wielding sophisticated weapons.
We’ve also seen them wearing Hawaiian shirts and carrying a basic handgun to empty the register in a liquor store, so the spectrum is well and truly there.
Rob Nelson explained in the interview:
These guys are a younger couple with their backs against the wall. Narratively, it doesn’t make a lot of sense for them to go out and cause as much carnage and make as much noise as they can.
Thanks to GameRoll on socials for the heads up.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is just a few days away from hitting the market. Are you looking forward to the game? Let us know your thoughts on the Insider Gaming Discord server .

articles.title_orig: Driver Stops in Front of Moving Car, Then Gets Mad When Motorist Goes Around: "Road Rage Or Insurance Scam?"
articles.title_zh: Driver Stops in Front of Moving Car, Then Gets Mad When Motorist Goes Around: "Road Rage Or Insurance Scam?"
articles.content_orig:
A driver traveling on a rain-soaked road had to stop suddenly when another motorist moved into their lane and slammed on the brakes. The close call was only the start of an encounter that soon drew thousands of reactions online.
Dashcam footage shared on Reddit on November 8 shows the confrontation on a suburban road. According to the person who posted the video, the other driver came to a complete stop, leaving little room to get around.
The motorist said the other driver began yelling and making rude gestures before following their vehicle. What started as a possible rear-end crash had turned into a confrontation that continued even after the cars separated.
Now, people watching the clip are arguing over what caused the strange behavior. Some suspect road rage, while others think the driver may have been trying to cause a crash for an insurance claim.
The original Reddit post , shared by u/pooh_jo in r/dashcams, describes a drive that took an unexpected turn.
The recording begins on a wet suburban road, with other vehicles traveling nearby. As the dashcam vehicle moves forward, another car enters its lane and slows sharply before coming to a stop.
The driver behind manages to avoid hitting it, but getting past is another problem. According to the person who posted the footage, they had to reverse before there was enough space to drive around the stopped vehicle.
Rather than simply continuing down the road, the other motorist reportedly became angry. The person behind the dashcam described the driver yelling, making an obscene gesture, and later flashing their headlights while following.
The person who posted the video could not explain why the other motorist behaved that way. In the original description, they wrote, "I have no idea if this was some sort of road rage or insurance scam."
That question quickly took over the comments. One Reddit user wrote, "Honestly seems like an Insurance scam." Others agreed, pointing to the wet pavement and sudden stop as reasons for concern.
Not everyone accepted that explanation. Some commenters thought the driver might have been upset about the dashcam vehicle's speed and was trying to force it to slow down.
Another viewer suggested that a person planning an insurance scam would likely have driven away once the attempted collision failed. The continued confrontation, in that user's view, looked more like someone trying to make a point.
Neither explanation has been established. The post contains no evidence of an insurance claim or a confirmed motive for the other driver's actions.
The discussion also turned toward the person recording the footage. Several commenters questioned whether the dashcam driver was traveling too quickly for the rainy conditions.
Others pushed back, arguing that the vehicle appeared to leave enough room for nearby traffic and that the driver responded carefully to the sudden stop. One commenter claimed the posted speed was only slightly above the road's limit, though that limit has not been independently confirmed.
The argument soon shifted from the dashcam vehicle's speed to whether either driver had the right to confront another motorist over their driving.
One commenter put it simply: "Explanation doesn't equal excuse."
The person who shared the footage did not report a collision in their description. Instead, they described escaping the stopped vehicle only to have the other driver flash their lights and follow afterward.

articles.title_orig: Delta CEO says air traffic control systems are so outdated that some routes were faster in the 1950s
articles.title_zh: Delta CEO says air traffic control systems are so outdated that some routes were faster in the 1950s
articles.content_orig:
The air traffic control tower at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in Los Angeles, California, on Nov. 14, 2026.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday blamed the previous day’s nationwide ground stop on the replacement of copper wires at a “remote” Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) facility. Installing new fiber optic lines led to critical communication breakdowns, he said.
About 7,500 flights were delayed and over 9,000 were canceled on Friday, according to FlightAware . Some 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. Eastern, shortly after the ground stop began.
The incident raised questions about what might have led to the historic event—only the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11—and what authorities were doing to prevent it from happening again.
“What we’re working to determine is whether we had incompetence or did they install a faulty router,” Duffy said Saturday, which saw nearly 6,000 additional flights canceled.
As investigators continued working to pinpoint the source of the problem, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters in Washington, D.C., that disrupted flight schedules were expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday and promised that the “worst is behind us.”
While that may be true for this specific outage, Duffy warned Friday that what happened was not an isolated incident and said that outages would likely continue to occur until antiquated communications equipment across the FAA’s air traffic control network was brought up to date.
“It was the old legacy equipment. It failed,” Duffy said. “And listen, it’s going to continue to fail.”
The Transportation Secretary went on to call for Congress to provide $50 billion before the end of the year to upgrade air traffic control and airport infrastructure, increasing the administration’s recent $30.1 billion request, which included $10.1 billion specifically for air traffic control modernization.
There is reason to believe, however, that financial support alone will not solve the problems currently faced by the FAA. Those include shortages in fully certified air traffic controllers, weaknesses in planning and coordinating necessary modernization work, and vulnerabilities to cybersecurity threats.
TIME has reached out to Duffy’s office for comment.
Modernizing the FAA’s air traffic control system has been a goal of the industry for years, says Edward Booth, an aviation attorney and pilot based in Jacksonville, and billions of dollars have already been sunk into the process.
“There has been a very methodical four-part, four-stage plan to upgrade that,” Booth tells TIME, referencing NextGen , a multibillion-dollar FAA modernization initiative dating to 2003. It has included shifting toward satellite-based aircraft tracking, digital communications, and more efficient flight routes.
Booth says a major focus of those earlier modernization efforts was making more efficient use of airspace.
“They have tried to squeeze more airplanes into limited space, make better use of the limited runways available in the system, and they started with completely changing the way airplanes are tracked in the world. It's a world standard now,” he says, pointing to how NextGen has already made strides in air travel.
The agency’s newer overhaul builds on earlier modernization work and includes replacing aging communications equipment, radar, and other infrastructure, with its first phase targeted for completion by the end of 2028.
“It's a very highly technical, robust system,” Booth says of the National Airspace System (NAS), “but it seems the weak spot was discovered yesterday afternoon.”
For more than two decades, the FAA has been working to modernize the NAS while fighting an uphill battle against aging infrastructure. The average U.S. air traffic control tower was 40 years old, and most radar systems were approaching that age, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Chairman Sam Graves wrote in a May 2025 op-ed .
Congress had already ordered an independent review of the FAA’s aging technology: The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required an audit of legacy systems deployed before 2000—including their vulnerability to single-point failures—and a plan to accelerate replacement or improvement of those found to pose risks. In a written response to Congress , the FAA said that nonprofit research organization MITRE completed the audit in August 2025. The response said the findings would guide modernization efforts, but did not disclose the specific findings or resulting actions.
In July 2025, Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA to upgrade its “radar, software, hardware, and telecommunications” at more than 4,600 sites through December 2028.
As of Nov. 5, the FAA said it has “replaced 69% of copper wires, installed Surface Awareness Initiative (SAI) systems at 143 towers, transitioned 26 towers to electronic flight strips [and] installed 226 IP Voice Switches.”
The updates were noted within an announcement saying the FAA was beginning to phase out the floppy disks used in air traffic control. It said that it had launched a replacement system that would include a digital display board with data about disruptions, weather conditions, and advisories. The announcement identified five initial facilities and set a goal of installing the system at 435 sites by the end of 2028.
Duffy called these efforts “the latest signal that America’s brand new air traffic control system is coming at lightning speed.”
The FAA then announced Nov. 10 that it was expanding its AI-powered scheduling and flight-planning tool—known as SMART (Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories)—to airspace managed by all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers nationwide. SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million contract that also covers the agency’s Flow Management Data and Services program.
Duffy said at Friday’s press conference that SMART had nothing to do with the disruption.
Describing Friday's outage, Duffy said a router being replaced as workers switched from copper wiring to fiber-optic connections began flooding other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting communications and some radar feeds. Systems came back online after officials isolated the work at the remote location, he said.
For Booth, the spread of that disruption underscores the need for safeguards that can contain a problem in one part of the FAA’s communications network before it affects the wider system.
“They need a system that is not prone to single-point failures,” he says.
Booth pointed out that legacy systems—often relying on analog lines, decades-old routers, and interconnected regional hubs—lack the fault-tolerant design needed to prevent a local or routine maintenance glitch from cascading nationwide.
“The public probably would be shocked to learn that the way pilots communicate with air traffic control is tantamount to an old-fashioned telephone line,” he says. “You've got 10, sometimes 15 airplanes competing to talk to a single controller-specified frequency.”
Kumar Sokka, the CEO of Acre Security, says a key consideration when upgrading complex systems is whether individual components can fail without disrupting the entire network.
“Can you remove a single point of failure? Are these systems distributed in a way where it's siloed in certain structures where if something fails, not everything fails, right?” asks Sokka.

articles.title_orig: Kim Jong Un Remakes North Korea’s Flag, Ditching Soviet-Era Version
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong Un Remakes North Korea’s Flag, Ditching Soviet-Era Version
articles.content_orig:
SEOUL, Nov. 13 (Yonhap) -- North Korea has revised its constitution to change its national flag's aspect ratio for the first time since its regime was established in 1948, according to the amended basic law posted on the website of Pyongyang's propaganda outlet.
Article 166 of the revised constitution posted on Naenara's website stipulates that the ratio of the flag's height to its width is 1 to 1.65, replacing the previous ratio of 1 to 2.
The change came as North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has sought to build his own governing style and national identity while retaining some legacies of his predecessors.
The flag's 1-to-2 ratio rule had remained unchanged in the law until the North's constitutional revision in September 2023.
Despite the ratio change, the overall design of the North's flag remains intact, consisting of a broad red stripe in the center, narrow white stripes above and below it, blue stripes above and below the white stripes, and a red five-pointed star in a white circle.
The constitution says the red stripe stands for the blood shed by anti-Japan fighters who dedicated their lives to defending the country's freedom and independence during Japan's 1910-45 colonial rule. The white circle and two white stripes symbolize people's loyalty to the nation's leader and ruling Workers' Party of Korea.
The two blue stripes represent the revolutionary spirit of the people struggling for peace, friendship and unity in the world, as well as the country's sovereignty, it said.
Observers said the change in the flag's aspect ratio might have reflected Pyongyang's efforts to craft a new national image under the incumbent leader Kim, the third-generation hereditary ruler.

articles.title_orig: Lord Mayor’s Show takes place through City of London streets
articles.title_zh: Lord Mayor’s Show takes place through City of London streets
articles.content_orig:
One of the floats is a replica of Tower Bridge
The new Lord Mayor of the City of London will travel along the Thames by barge on Saturday, reviving a centuries-old tradition before the annual Lord Mayor's Show, as artists put the finishing touches to the flotilla.
Lord Mayor Bronek Masojada will leave Westminster at 08:30 GMT aboard the ceremonial barge Jubilant, followed by a flotilla of livery company boats, before coming ashore at HMS President.
The barge journey echoes the route Lord Mayors once took to Westminster to swear loyalty to the Crown.
About 6,500 people, 250 horses and more than 50 floats, including a replica of Tower Bridge with rising bascules - movable sections of road - are to be involved in the event.
Creative director Rachel Grunwald has been overseeing the project
They will then take part in the 2.86-mile (4.6km) procession, which leaves Mansion House at 11:00 and travels to the Royal Courts of Justice and back.
About a dozen artists have been working on the bridge float at Emergency Exit Arts in Greenwich, and creative director Rachel Grunwald said it held some surprises.
"You can see the workings of the mechanism that used to open up the bridge, and you can see cats inside that used to be employed to catch the rats," she said.
"You've got a double-decker bus on the float, because of a double-decker bus that jumped the bridge in 1952 . We've got an elephant because the viewing deck can take the weight of six elephants."
Amy West, one of the artists, is working on the detail around the windows inside the bridge.
"It's a very tricky interior to do because there's so many beautiful steps that go up through Tower Bridge, but we're trying to put some of the details around the windows," she said.
Artist Amy West has been working on the bridge windows
Grunwald added that the float had taken half a year to build.
"We've had a team on this for the last six months, and over the last couple of months in this building we've had about 10 or 12 artists bringing it together," she said.
Chris Earlie, director of Tower Bridge, said: "This is quite accurate as far as the bascules are concerned. It's even got the design, the steelwork there, and they are articulated in that they can actually raise."
Alongside the bridge in the Greenwich workshop is a towering red-and-white lighthouse representing the Honourable Company of Master Mariners.
Masojada, who came to the UK from South Africa, takes office at the Silent Ceremony on Friday. He succeeds Dame Susan Langley, the first person to hold the title of Lady Mayor, and will be London's 698th Lord Mayor.
Organisers, who expect more than 350,000 people to line the route, are urging visitors to use public transport because of widespread road closures.

articles.title_orig: Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%
articles.title_zh: Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%
articles.content_orig:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.
Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.
The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.
The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.
Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August .
Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.
After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.
They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.
Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.
We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q , released last Saturday , indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.
It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.
As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.
On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.
Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.
If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.
The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."
The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.
Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders .
In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.
Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each , and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.
That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.
The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.
Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.
In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.
All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.
In a term sheet filed early Friday , Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.
Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.
It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.
In April , Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.
Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.
Some links may require a subscription:
Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, " The Intelligent Investor ," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.
WARREN BUFFETT : On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, " Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits " and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.
You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] " The Intelligent Investor ," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.
Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...
One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.
And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.
And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s spy scandal isn’t a one-off
articles.content_orig:

Jensen Huang and President Trump at a 2025 White House event. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
The world's most powerful AI executive admitted Sunday to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, sending shock waves through an industry built on his singular influence.
Why it matters: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has fashioned himself as the indispensable leader of an indispensable company — a $4.5 trillion behemoth with unparalleled clout in Silicon Valley, on Wall Street and inside President Trump's White House.
The big picture: Huang, who has led Nvidia since founding the chipmaker 33 years ago, has become the AI boom's chief evangelist and most authoritative voice.
Driving the news: Huang confessed to the affair in a letter to staff Sunday, apologizing to his family as Nvidia's board launched an independent probe into the suspected Chinese intelligence operation.
Zoom in: The New York Times first exposed the suspected Chinese espionage operation on Oct. 29, reporting that a woman believed to be working for Beijing had developed a close relationship with Nvidia's CEO.
The intrigue: The Trump administration reportedly knew about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation long before it became public.
Reality check: There's no public evidence that Huang's relationship influenced his advocacy for selling to China, a longstanding commercial priority for Nvidia.
What to watch: Huang's scandal comes amid a dramatic reversal of political fortunes for the AI industry, as voters rejected data center expansion and handed control of Congress to Democrats promising tougher oversight.

articles.title_orig: The Microsoft outage didn’t lose your email — here’s what it does mean for you
articles.title_zh: The Microsoft outage didn’t lose your email — here’s what it does mean for you
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Millions of office workers got an unplanned break from email Thursday. Their bosses' favorite new AI tool got one too.
A Microsoft ( MSFT ) outage that began midday Thursday knocked out Outlook and other workplace apps worldwide, with Downdetector logging reports from 74 countries within about an hour. By Friday, Microsoft said it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress."
The damage reached Microsoft's AI. Copilot couldn't access users' email, files, or calendars, and the Microsoft connectors for OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) Claude broke too.
Microsoft says more than 430 million people use its Microsoft 365 apps.
Your email isn't lost. Microsoft stretched its email timeout to 48 hours , so messages sent to you keep trying to deliver instead of bouncing back.
There isn't much to fix on your end. Resetting your password or reinstalling Outlook won't help, though desktop Outlook may still show mail it already downloaded.
If your company pays for Microsoft 365, it may be owed money. Microsoft promises 99.9% uptime , about 43 minutes of downtime a month, with credits of 25% to 100% of the monthly fee when it falls short. Your IT department has to file the claim.
Microsoft is hard to replace, which is usually good news for its shareholders. Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman, whose fund owns Microsoft stock, said at Yahoo Finance Invest on Thursday that Microsoft is "the gateway to how people interact with the basic workflows of a desk worker," which makes it "a much more difficult position to dislodge."
This week showed the other side of that.
Microsoft has blamed its own changes or maintenance for Microsoft 365 disruptions in at least six months this year, from a nearly 10-hour outage in January to a spam-filter update that bounced real email earlier this month.
Australia's home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said Microsoft believes it's dealing with "an update that has gone awry," much like the 2024 CrowdStrike meltdown.
Microsoft reached for the oldest fix in the help desk manual, saying Thursday it was "restarting affected servers to return them to service."
It didn't stick. Servers that came back went down again once traffic returned. On Friday, Microsoft traced the outage to a problem from "an earlier network capacity upgrade" that surfaced after a recent network change, and said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption."
The outage comes as Microsoft trims its workforce while spending heavily on AI. It offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees in October, and those who accept leave Dec. 31. CEO Satya Nadella said last year that AI writes "maybe 20%, 30%" of Microsoft's code .
Microsoft says AI wasn't the culprit. It called the outage "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents" in a post on X . In a statement to Yahoo Finance, Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, said the company regrets "the impact these outages had on those who depend on us" and that "our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward." He didn't address questions about staffing.
Chris Versace, chief investment officer at Tematica Research, put the lesson simply: "The outage and how it hobbled many businesses and other enterprises is a reminder about the need for redundancies."
Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication.
Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. Follow him on X at @SPYJared or email him at jaredblikre@yahooinc.com .

articles.title_orig: Nearly €20m in cash found buried, hidden in Hungary corruption case
articles.title_zh: Nearly €20m in cash found buried, hidden in Hungary corruption case
articles.content_orig:
Anti-corruption agency carried out searches as part of investigation into Orbán-era minister accused of taking bribes
Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth $19.5m (£14.8m) buried in forests and hidden elsewhere while investigating an ex-minister of nationalist former leader Viktor Orbán’s cabinet.
Miklós Seszták, Hungary’s minister of national development between 2014 and 2018, is accused of taking bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company, purchasing secondhand buses at inflated prices.
The prime minister, Péter Magyar , won a landslide election victory in April, ending Orbán’s 16 years in power after promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during his rival’s rule.
Seszták, two other Orbán-era ministers and the former premier’s brother have been taken into custody in different cases as graft inquiries have gathered pace in recent weeks.
The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), an anti-graft body with sweeping powers established as part of Magyar’s accountability drive, said it searched several locations on Thursday and Friday as part of the criminal proceedings against Seszták.
“During the search, investigators found large amounts of cash: buried in forests, hidden in agricultural and warehouse buildings as well as residential properties, and stored in high-value safes in secluded locations,” the statement said.
“The total amount of cash found during the two-day search was 5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and US $1,257,100,” it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m.
NVVH said its staff deposited the cash into the Hungarian State Treasury’s account.
“Upon receipt, 12 Treasury employees spent 8 hours counting the money using 5 counting machines,” the finance minister, András Kármán, said on Facebook.
Magyar hailed the seizure as a potential turning point.
“This officially marks the end of the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” he said in reference to Orbán’s former governing coalition.
The former leader did not react to the latest development. Orbán had previously denounced the probes targeting his inner circle as “political persecution” aimed at imprisoning him.

articles.title_orig: Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
articles.title_zh: Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
articles.content_orig:
Records leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, have shown that at least 450,000 Russians, most of them soldiers, died in the war in Ukraine up to August this year.
Among the dead were more than 4,000 foreign citizens who are believed to have died fighting for Russia, from countries including Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Nepal, Colombia and Nigeria.
The records were obtained by two hacking groups, the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Ukraine’s Silent Crow.
Rosstat confirmed it had been hit by cyberattacks between October 29 and November 1, but said it found no evidence that its databases had been compromised or that protected data leaked.
Moscow does not officially publish its military death toll.
Deaths can take months, and sometimes years, to be registered, in Russia. Investigations for The Financial Times (FT) have concluded that once late paperwork is counted, the toll up to August will settle at about 550,000.
So what do the leaked records show, and what do they tell us about who is fighting Russia’s war? Here’s what you need to know:
The Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow said on November 1 that they had broken into Rosstat’s network.
The two hacking groups published their own analysis of the records and shared the files with several news organisations, though the data has not been independently verified.
However, media outlets and analysts say they believe it is real.
Janis Kluge, an expert on Russia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, wrote on X: “There is no longer any doubt that the leaked Rosstat database is authentic. You can find any famous person who has died in recent years.”
However, in a later post he added: “The trickier question is: Was the data manipulated to increase the war death toll?” before adding, “This would [be] unbelievably difficult, so this is a highly unlikely conspiracy theory”.
A death toll far beyond anything Moscow has admitted so far.
The files list about 410,000 deaths directly as war-related, and 42,000 more fighting-age men whose deaths were confirmed in court because their bodies have never been recovered.
The FT identified another 12,000 likely military deaths among men who died at or near the front, bringing the total to at least 450,000.
About 120,000 of those with a recorded location died in the area containing Avdiivka and Pokrovsk, and a further 48,000 in Bakhmut, the FT reported.
Avdiivka is a small industrial city in the Donetsk region. After Russian-backed forces seized parts of eastern Ukraine in 2014 and 2015, it became part of the so-called “contact line”, and Ukrainian forces spent years fortifying the city.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it was the subject of two years of bitter fighting before Russia took it in 2024.
After the fall of Avdiivka, Russian forces moved towards the coal-mining city of Pokrovsk in the Donetsk region, capturing it in early 2026 after more than a year of gruelling battles that had left the city in ruins.
Bakhmut, a city in the Donetsk Oblast and situated at a vital intersection connecting eastern Ukraine with the rest of the country, was the site of the longest and bloodiest infantry battle of the war before falling to Russian and paramilitary Wagner Group forces in May 2023.
Older men from poorer, often minority regions.
The average age of those killed rose from 34 in the first year of the war to 40 in 2025, and men aged 35 to 44 made up the largest group, with 158,000 dead, the FT reported.
Ethnic Russians constitute more than two-thirds of Russia’s population of 143 million. The rest are minorities – from millions of ethnic Ukrainians and Tatars to smaller Indigenous groups in Siberia and the Arctic.
Zabaykalsky Krai, home to a large community of Buryats, an Indigenous Mongolic people of southern Siberia, recorded about 12,300 deaths, roughly one for every 80 people in the region, the FT reported.
Bashkortostan, another region with a large minority population including Indigenous Bashkirs and Volga Tatars, recorded 15,800 deaths.
More than 4,000, and possibly far more.
The FT identified 4,141 probable foreign soldiers holding foreign citizenship among the dead.
Bloomberg News, using a wider definition that includes people born outside Russia, counted 11,335, with foreign deaths rising from about 630 in 2022 to more than 5,500 in 2025.
Deaths of Nepalis were concentrated in 2023 and 2024, and those of Colombians, Kenyans and Nigerians from late 2025, Bloomberg reported.
The FT counted the highest death toll from Uzbekistan at 807, followed by Tajikistan with 598. There were also 44 Nepali dead and 98 Colombians, the highest toll from Latin America.
About 340 Africans are among the dead, most of them killed since 2025, Bloomberg reported.
Nigeria, Cameroon and Egypt had the highest tolls, with 127 deaths between them, according to the FT.
Furthermore, Ukrainian officials believe Russia deployed some 14,000 North Korean troops to hold off Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into the Kursk region, but they do not appear in the leaked data.
Mostly for the money, and often after being misled.
An estimated 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries are said to be fighting in the Russian army overall.
An Amnesty International report in September found that people from Brazil, Colombia, Sri Lanka and South Africa had been promised well-paid civilian jobs and then forced into the army on arrival in Russia.
The rights group spoke with foreign nationals currently serving with Russian forces and members of their families as well as lawyers, human rights activists and journalists.
It found local agents and misleading online job advertisements were being used to deceive foreign nationals in their home countries.
Nationals from 36 African countries are known to be fighting for Russia in the four-year war, Ukraine’s foreign minister said in November last year.
One South African man who applied online for a driving job in Poland was told to fly to Moscow, pick up a truck, and drive it to Poland.
His wife told Amnesty International: “Upon arrival to Moscow, everything was taken from him. He was told that he would not be going to Poland and that he is becoming a soldier.”
Many recruits were promised lucrative salaries and sign-up bonuses that were not then fulfilled, Amnesty reported.
In Kenya , where intelligence officials say more than 1,000 citizens have been recruited, agencies promised monthly wages of about $2,715 and bonuses of up to $9,309.
Moscow denies coercing anyone to fight in Ukraine.
They indicate that Russia is struggling for manpower.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, posted an analysis of the leaked data, saying the figures likely understate Russia’s true losses because of reporting limitations.
It added that, as of July, Russia’s casualties are now outpacing its recruitment.
Kluge told The Moscow Times that the deaths also represent about half a per cent of Russia’s working-age population, which may have little economic impact, so the main significance is political.
He added, “You cannot say Russia is winning this war if it is losing population at this rate.”

articles.title_orig: China holds 80% of underwater data center patents in past 20 years, can boost AI energy use
articles.title_zh: China holds 80% of underwater data center patents in past 20 years, can boost AI energy use
articles.content_orig:
China owns around 80 percent of all global underwater data center patents.
Two Chinese researchers analyzing 168 patents filed between 2006 and 2026 reported this finding.
They also found that China holds the lion's share, with South Korea owning around 17, and the rest split between the US and Europe.
A new study has found that China owns around 80 percent of all global underwater data center patents. That’s not to say China owns much of the technology used in these setups, but it does reveal how active it has been in patenting in this field.
The study’s findings come from two Chinese researchers analyzing 168 patents filed between 2006 and 2026. It appears to show that technological focus has shifted quite dramatically over this time.
Before about 2014, patents were dominated by American, Norwegian, and Canadian researchers exploring underwater enclosures and pressure protection. Between about 2015 and 2020, attention turned to cooling, electrical supply, and long-term reliability.
From 2021, Chinese researchers became the dominant source for patents, particularly focusing on modular construction and maintenance. They also found that China holds the lion’s share, with South Korea owning around 17, and the rest split between the US and Europe.
Chinese patents in particular focus on the actual construction, installation, connections, and maintenance of them at scale. This appears to show that China is shifting focus to the more practical elements rather than proving experimental technology.
All very interesting, but why all the interest? Well, data centers generate an enormous amount of heat when in operation. This comes from the conversion of electricity into heat by the vast number of computer processors.
Typically, this is handled by using a combination of fans, chillers, cooling towers, and liquid-cooling systems to manage temperatures. That is costly in terms of hardware and additional electricity costs.
If the centers could be placed underwater, they could take advantage of the ocean’s near-limitless supply of very cold seawater. Obviously, you can’t just submerge the hardware directly into the ocean, so they need to be placed inside sealed, pressure-resistant containers first.
These are then lowered and secured to the seabed, and connections are made to the shore for power and data cables. Once there, the heat from the servers can be transferred to the cold ocean water using special internal cooling systems.
To this end, the seawater acts as a massive heat sink, potentially eliminating much of the mechanical cooling equipment needed on land. This doesn’t make the computers themselves consume less electricity, but it can reduce the energy spent keeping them cool.
And it is not just a theoretical technology either. Famously, Microsoft deployed one, called Project Natick , off the coast of Scotland in 2018. The project ran for around two years, and results were very encouraging.
According to Microsoft, the underwater data center had just one-eighth of the failure rate of similar land-based setups. Yet despite this, Microsoft chose not to commercialize the technology, and confirmed in 2024 that the project had been discontinued.
So, is the 80 percent figure something other nations should sit up and take notice of? Yes, and no. It is clear China has established some kind of lead here in terms of patents, but the engineering challenges of actually deploying them are enormous.
The shift in focus to modularity likely reflects China’s ambitions to scale the technology commercially. But it is important to note that patents tend to be territorial in nature.
Holding a large share of patents in a particular field doesn’t automatically give a country control of the technology worldwide.
Christopher graduated from Cardiff University in 2004 with a Masters Degree in Geology. articles.title_orig: The Surprise Censorship Battle Over My Cocktail Book Has Left Me Shaken—and Stirred
articles.title_zh: The Surprise Censorship Battle Over My Cocktail Book Has Left Me Shaken—and Stirred
articles.content_orig:
DEAR ABBY : My sister-in-law “Leah” has been a poor money manager all her life. She is in significant credit card debt and had to borrow money to help pay for her wedding, despite the fact that she has been a teacher for decades. She has never been a saver — always a spender.
When my husband passed away recently, he left me with $1 million in life insurance proceeds. When Leah found out about it (I’m not sure how), she asked me to lend her some money to get back on her feet. When I refused, my other sister-in-law chastised me, saying that my husband would have lent her the money. Leah has been bailed out a few times by her sister but never by my husband. Am I wrong to stand my ground? — NOT AN ENABLER
DEAR NOT AN ENABLER : My heart goes out to you for the loss of your husband. Leah may be using the word “lend,” but believe me when I say you would never see that money again. If she wants to get out of debt, she needs to speak to a credit counselor, not her brother’s grieving widow. If she brings it up again, tell her to visit the National Foundation for Credit Counseling at nfcc.org.
DEAR ABBY : I am a 70-year-old divorced man. For the past 10 years, my ex-wife has been living with me. Due to her medical condition and lack of family support, she has no one else to assist her. My own health is declining, so caring for her is a physical strain and emotionally stressful. She refuses any suggestion of a senior living facility because her only income is a small Social Security benefit.
How do I move on without fighting and accusations? I know I facilitated this by allowing her into my home in the first place. Any ideas where to begin? — FRUSTRATED IN TEXAS
DEAR FRUSTRATED : You were kind to take in and care for your ex a decade ago, but this arrangement is now affecting your health. To protect your own well-being, you must put your foot down. Help your ex-wife one last time by finding her a facility she can afford. Do not expect the transition to be pleasant, but the result will be an improvement for both of you.
DEAR ABBY : I am a happily married woman who went through a midlife crisis more than 20 years ago. At the time, I left my husband for another man, who gave me an expensive cocktail ring. When my relationship with the new man started to suffer for various reasons, I returned to my husband. Our marriage has remained strong ever since.
I have never worn the ring and have always felt guilty for having it. Should I contact my former lover and return it? Should I pawn it and send him the proceeds? Or maybe you have another suggestion? — RINGS HOLLOW IN ARIZONA
DEAR RINGS HOLLOW : Sell the ring and donate the proceeds to a worthy charitable cause. Do not open the door to further contact with your former lover.
Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at http://www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.

articles.title_orig: China Spy Claims Expose Global Tech Espionage
articles.title_zh: China Spy Claims Expose Global Tech Espionage
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's now ex-CEO left the post after it emerged he was romantically involved with a woman alleged to be spying for China, jolting the U.S. AI surge and thrusting allegations of Chinese penetration at major Western tech firms into the spotlight .
Beijing rejected the claims as a smear and said Washington is inventing "Chinese spy narratives" to rationalize curbs on technology exports. Even so, the operative suspected of involvement in the episode that precipitated Huang 's exit is currently in China and the Chinese government is aware of her presence.
What hangs in the balance is economic and military clout. The U.S. is betting a lead in AI and advanced chips will sustain its strength and help deter China over Taiwan, while espionage offers Beijing a way to narrow that lead and glean insight into U.S. military plans and political decision-making.
German prosecutors report that a married pair posed as interpreters and auto-sector workers to court academics across AI, computer science and aerospace, flying some to China to give paid "civilian" talks for state-owned defense companies.
According to New Zealand intelligence, a Chinese observatory closely linked to the government attempted to set up space-tracking gear via a domestic firm, equipment that might double as a tool for gathering military intelligence. Taiwan says Chinese agents trawl social media to find soldiers in debt, extend loans, and then demand sensitive information and referrals to fellow service members.
The Philippines offers a closer look at scale and sophistication. Authorities say suspected Chinese operatives claimed they flew drones loaded with fishing bait while observing warships near Subic Bay, and that another group pretended to be seafood purchasers as they piloted drones close to a naval installation. In Manila, contracted drivers equipped their cars with sham cellphone towers and cruised by the presidential palace, military encampments and the U.S. Embassy to scoop up nearby phone data.
A separate car outfitted with cameras plus mapping gear made stops at more than 120 sites, among them bases used by American forces. Officials add that presumed operatives cultivated sources within the defense establishment to secure rosters of naval personnel, timetables for troop rotations and resupply, and details on missions to outposts in the disputed South China Sea.
An investigator told Bloomberg the network encompassed hundreds. China has rejected the allegations as baseless.
In uncertain times, thoughtful investors look for reliable ways to sharpen their edge. We're hosting our first ever investor livestream on 11/17 to show you how to use ChatGPT and Claude to invest like a pro, hosted by Briefs Finance CEO Jaspreet Singh. Save your seat .
Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said the activity is widespread and not confined to the Philippines, pointing to cases in the United States, Australia and the United Kingdom.
Security agencies are turning up the volume. According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Chinese espionage is "a grave threat to the economic well-being" of the U.S. Britain's MI5 reported that in 2022 it was handling seven times the number of China-related probes as it had four years before. Canadian intelligence describes China as its "greatest counter-intelligence threat," while Dutch intelligence reports that Chinese digital espionage targeting technology firms is occurring on a "large scale."
China's Ministry of State Security is central to this push, combining overseas and domestic roles and, under Xi Jinping, tightening control over local bureaus to coordinate nationwide and pursue more ambitious missions abroad. Under the 2017 National Intelligence Law, every organization and citizen must "support, assist, and cooperate" with intelligence work.
Holden Triplett, who once led the FBI's Beijing office, said Chinese services have become highly professional, increasingly exploit human vulnerabilities, and that anyone can be susceptible.
With the AI revolution in full swing, Western officials say Chinese spy agencies have prioritized the technology that underpins it, seeking it through hacking and human sources.
AI is also changing tradecraft. "Human espionage doesn't anymore have to be sneaking around back alleys."
AI is also boosting cyber operations.
The bottom line: Washington is counting on AI and advanced chips to preserve economic and military heft, and the alleged espionage drive aims at those very advantages.

articles.title_orig: US officials raise alarm over restricted Nvidia AI chips reaching China
articles.title_zh: US officials raise alarm over restricted Nvidia AI chips reaching China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."
